Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.
  • It has been revealed that existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million).
  • Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

It has been revealed that existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Recent findings suggest that fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

It has been revealed that “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun mentioned in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

Recent findings suggest that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant stated mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

In a recent development, “So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant noted. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he mentioned. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun stated in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

Sources indicate that “Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she remarked. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale stated jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she stated. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun mentioned rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

Sources indicate that however, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

Industry observers note that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on upcoming pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”.

#110686. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2176 w)

The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • Recent findings suggest that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

Recent findings suggest that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Recent findings suggest that key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

In a recent development, the millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

Sources indicate that “For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s notable to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” remarked Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

Sources indicate that millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another substantial expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

According to recent reports, adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

Industry observers note that but their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners stated they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

In a recent development, consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Industry observers note that home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

It has been revealed that share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

It has been revealed that as a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

According to recent reports, on this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

According to recent reports, he explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel notable.

They also get into handling rejection, taking major risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy states many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

Industry observers note that for agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are settling into life in their fresh home in the Cotswalds, and according to the Duchess of Sussex's wedding hairstylist, George Northwood, the grass is looking very green in the United Kingdom.

Northwood shared a look inside the family's latest digs in a Nov. 22 Instagram post, noting that he and Markle had recently spent quite a bit of quality time together, including a lunch date and a visit to her new property.

During an early fall trip to Markle's abode, Northwood remarked they "picked fruit and vegetables" from her garden. The stylist has recently welcomed a son, seven-month-old Elijah, "who has just started weaning" and is exploring fresh foods.

It has been revealed that "She was very excited for all the new flavors he was going to enjoy from the garden," Northwood recalled. "I remember Archie being the same age when we went on tour to South Africa, so it was a lovely circular moment.".

Later, the duo would head to The Park Restaurant—a Upcoming York-inspired eatery just blocks from Kensington Palace. In a blog on the eatery's website, Northwood divulged more about their catchup.

"I invited Meghan as she has just come back to the U.K. and, though we have stayed in touch via text, we hadn’t had the chance to have a proper download yet," Northwood noted of their lunch date. "Since we last saw each other, she’s had her second baby and I’ve had my first. Catching up was like old times, when we used to have dinner together when I accompanied her on royal tours around the world.".

Northwood added that Markle—who he refers to as "M"—is a wonderful lunch companion because she is "someone with good chat who enjoys a laugh and, crucially, who wants to share the food so that I get to try a bit of everything.".

The pals enjoyed sea bass, French fries, and key lime pie. Northwood noted that "Meghan was happy to go along" with his pescatarian diet.

He also noted that "there is a lot of baby chat" given his recent "solo surrogacy journey," and that he's picked up plenty of "parenting tips" from the mom of two.

Northwood also shared a sweet photo of Markle smiling with his son at her home, posed beside a basket of colorful garden-picked veggies.

Markle, 45, and Harry, 42, are reported to be residing in a property on an estate belonging to their close friends, according to the Daily Mail.

They first made aims to establish a private residence in the U.K. in August of this year, six years after quitting their roles as working members of the British royal family to relocate to a $14.7 million home in Montecito, CA.

Although it was recently reported that the seemingly unexpected move was motivated by visa troubles for Harry—with a US government source telling Page Six "his visa expired and wasn't immediately renewed"—the couple's spokesperson denied the claim, telling Newsweek it is "entirely false.".

In an October interview with GQ, Harry expressed that the decision was driven by a desire to seek out "opportunities for the family.".

"Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me," he said of Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. "I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it and it’s just giving them a whole different experience.".

He also admitted that "it's nice to be back" on "U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there.".

The family looks to stay put for the holidays, marking the children's first British Christmas.

During a Nov. 20 appearance on the British morning show, "This Morning," Harry revealed the family's aims for Thanksgiving and Christmas, noting that mother-in-law Doria Ragland will be joining them.

"My wife is very good in the kitchen and so is my mother-in-law, so I'll leave that to them," he said, noting that he hopes turkey and gumbo are on the menu.

The decision to stay in England for the holidays also comes from a desire to keep things simple during a difficult time for Markle's family, as her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been indicted in Florida on two counts of possession of child pornography.

Sources indicate that "Everything going on with her dad is still weighing heavily on her," a source told People. "She wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family.

"Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone," the source added.

UPDATED 20:54 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

Industry observers note that in a letter to manufacturer employees, Ramaswami (pictured) stated he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.

Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

According to recent reports, “Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this company and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”.

It has been revealed that ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the organization delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

The firm reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

Nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the manufacturer guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

Investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

Virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the tech giant during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she said. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”.

In a recent development, in a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami stated he believes the manufacturer is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

“[We have] transformed the tech giant to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami remarked. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”.

According to Ramaswami, Nutanix now stands at an inflection point as it looks to cash in on the newly introduced era of artificial intelligence. “I’ve been talking to the board for a bit about this, as well as in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession, and so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time,” he told analysts. “[We wanted] to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader.”.

In a recent development, ramaswami’s departure from the organization should at least be a lot smoother than his arrival. Nutanix announced it had appointed Ramaswami as its CEO in late 2020, just two days after he quit his role as chief operating officer of its biggest rival, VMware.

In a recent development, VMware was indignant about the manner of his departure, and responded with a lawsuit that accused Ramaswami of breaching his legal and contractual duties to the tech giant by “secretly meeting” with Nutanix’s board to discuss taking over, while continuing to play a leading role in shaping its product and business strategy. The lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court about a year later.

In April, Ramaswami appeared on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s mobile livestreaming studio, where he talked about how Nutanix is shifting away from HCI to focus on more of a “disaggregated infrastructure” strategy to support demand for autonomous AI agents:.

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of substantial news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

According to recent reports, the Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Industry observers note that finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are Fresh York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Recent findings suggest that crypto exchange Binance has issued a "one-letter" security warning to crypto customers, urging them to carefully check website addresses before logging into their accounts. According to Binance, a fake site can be just one letter off.

A post on X by the crypto exchange pointed out that a small difference in a website URL, sometimes just one letter, can lead customers to visit fake websites impersonating legitimate platforms.

"Sometimes the biggest red flag is just one letter," Binance wrote.

The exchange advised users to double-check URLs before entering their login credentials. It also encouraged anyone uncertain about a website's authenticity to use Binance's official verification tool to confirm whether the URL belongs to the platform.

The Binance Verify platform allows crypto consumers to stay safe from scammers, as they can enter a URL, email address, phone number, Telegram account, or social media account to check if the source is verified and officially from Binance.

It has been revealed that impersonation scams are quietly growing across the crypto space, with one of the most troubling tactics seen being the deepfake: lifelike, AI-generated impersonations of crypto executives and employees soliciting money on video calls that look and sound real enough to make anyone hesitate. The personas are fabricated, but the sophistication is genuine.

Every day, people are contacted by impersonators using the names, likenesses, and even job titles of crypto personnel, including Binance staff, to solicit investments or financial transactions via WhatsApp, Telegram, and other channels.

Binance stated that scammers prey on people's growing interest in investing and digital finance and on their trust, often masquerading as its employees or executives to exploit its credibility.

With advances in AI and deepfake technology, they can create personas that look and sound real. Crypto people are therefore urged to beware of unsolicited advice or "special opportunities" and to refrain from clicking on unknown links or URLs.

The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients.
  • Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place.
  • Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in Upcoming York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

It has been revealed that that shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an notable question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Recent findings suggest that going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

Recent findings suggest that the mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

Sources indicate that when a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

Sources indicate that A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Recent findings suggest that invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

According to recent reports, as brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

According to recent reports, local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stunning 1929 English Tudor home in Greensboro, NC, that gained notoriety after it appeared in "Hoarders" closed last week for $3.85 million after two years on the market.

The home was built during the Gilded Age for prominent local businessman Julian Price, and designed by Newly introduced York architect Charles C. Hartmann.

The 8,616-square-foot home, found at 301 Fisher Park Circle in Greensboro, has over 30 rooms, including eight bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and two half bathrooms.

The Julian Price Home was put on the National Register of Historic Place in 1980, it gained attention in 2017, when it was featured on an episode of A&E’s "Hoarders".

Recent findings suggest that the home was owned, at the time, by interior designer Sandra Cowart. She had lived in the home since 1975, and kept the home in pristine condition for years, even giving tours and renting out rooms, according to a 2017 article from the Chicago Tribune.

In a recent development, after 2005, she became closed off, became a compulsive collector, and her home was ultimately foreclosed on. The home was purchased out of foreclosure by Eric and Michael Fuko-Rizzo for $415,000, a fraction of the property’s value.

The couple transformed the home back to its former glory with their deep knowledge and love of old homes and architecture.

Sources indicate that “They were great people to re-do it, Eric and Michael. Michael’s energy and knowledge of loving old places is honestly over the top,” listing agent Kay Chesnutt, of Berkshire Hathaway Home Services, told Realtor.com. “Not many people would even consider redoing something or saving something like that.”.

According to recent reports, in addition to its numerous bedrooms, the home has an elaborate butlers' pantry, library, great room, and breakfast room. For sunny North Carolina days, there  is also a sunroom and a screened porch. All of the details were restored with intention and care for the home’s history.

“It’s like walking into a magical part of history. The beauty of the details and how they were restored—or, if they had to remove something, they’d replicate it,” Chesnutt described the restoration process. “It is something that should be saved for Greensboro. Anybody that goes into it says ‘Wow,’ because the pictures don’t even do it justice.

In a recent development, after the restoration, the Fuko-Rizzos opened the home up as an inn. At times, the home would be rented out in its entirety by families or host community events. It even received visits from stars like Carrie Underwood and Leanne Morgan, according to Chesnutt.

“Unwind in our drawing room with a book and glass of wine while observing the detail of the original molded plaster ceiling and fireplace surround,” the inn’s website reads. “However you plan your visit, it is certain that the charm, elegance and restored original details of this 1929 Tudor mansion will captivate and leave you and your guests with lasting memories.”.

The Fuko-Rizzos listed the home for sale again in August of 2024, for an initial price of $5.25 million.

Industry observers note that the property’s operation as an inn is one of the reasons that such a stunning home would remain on the market for two years, Chesnutt said. As the listing agent, she and the owners would have to coordinate showings around room availability.

“We couldn’t show it when there were people that were registered and paying guests. Their rooms were locked, so we only indicated it when times were open, and it was empty and clean and always immaculate,” remarked Chesnutt.

It has been revealed that after over two years, the home closed on November 19 for $3.85 million. The new owners are a local couple.

“It just suited them,” stated Chesnutt. “And I think they’ll be good care takers.”.

Industry observers note that chesnutt could not disclose whether the the newly introduced owners proposal to keep the property open as an inn or make it a family home, but the property is no longer active on Airbnb. Either way, the Julian Price Home has a long life ahead of it due to good bones and quality craftsmanship.

According to recent reports, “It has a wonderful feeling, and even on the darkest days, it’s very light,” said Chesnutt. “And the quality that was done then, we couldn’t reproduce today.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

According to recent reports, the October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

Industry observers note that the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

Recent findings suggest that at October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

Industry observers note that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh remarked in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

In a recent development, adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

Industry observers note that the number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

Recent findings suggest that the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

Recent findings suggest that the median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

Sources indicate that the October data overall indicates an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

  • Industry observers note that in a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, Upcoming York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Manhattan judge has upheld Newly introduced York City's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined.

Industry observers note that in a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, Upcoming York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T. Lantry found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its authority when it voted this summer to freeze rents on both one- and two-year leases.

The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy.

Industry observers note that despite the favorable ruling, Lantry wasn't entirely sympathetic to the mayor. In his final decision, he called Mamdani's campaign promise "reckless and irresponsible." Even so, he concluded that the board had independently considered the evidence before reaching its decision.

The freeze passed in June after a landmark 7-1 vote, with only Arpit Gupta, an economist who was appointed to the board in 2022 by Mayor Eric Adams, voting no.

It has been revealed that but it was owner-representative Maksim Wynn's statement that stoked controversy at the meeting, after he raised concerns about the financial health of the city's buildings. Wynn's full statement was drowned out by boos from the crowd before he ultimately voted in favor of the freeze.

Those pressures were central to the landlords' suit, which argued that a "rent freeze is impossible to reconcile" with such rising costs, pointing to mounting expenses for insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property taxes.

Operating and maintenance expenses consumed roughly 71 cents of every dollar of revenue in 2024, according to the board's 2026 Income and Expense Study. And as Realtor.com® previously reported, those figures exclude mortgage payments and major capital expenses, which landlords argue can leave otherwise profitable-looking buildings struggling financially.

“Freezing rent sounds like a sure-fire way to solve housing affordability, but what I'm worried about is the unintended consequences on the rent-stabilized stock and market-rate prices,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in June.

Lantry acknowledged that potential fallout, writing that the freeze could have "detrimental impacts on the New York City residential real estate industry." But he emphasized that weighing the wisdom of the policy was not the court's role, writing that the freeze "has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid.".

The ruling leaves the freeze intact; however, the landlords could seek to appeal.

#110670. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1080 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • Sources indicate that access is a good thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Sources indicate that access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely indicates you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

Recent findings suggest that this fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

Recent findings suggest that how to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

It has been revealed that real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

It has been revealed that in real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

In a recent development, if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

Industry observers note that how to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Sources indicate that now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Sources indicate that many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The firm running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

In a recent development, how to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the organization itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Sources indicate that many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your blueprint, not the floor under it.

According to recent reports, the average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis.
  • Prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026.
  • Industry observers note that this is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

Prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

Industry observers note that this is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

According to recent reports, home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

However, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”.

Sources indicate that there’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” said Zhao.

Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

Home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

According to recent reports, the biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

Recent findings suggest that on a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

According to recent reports, the biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

This report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

Sources indicate that in many cases, a health diagnosis can be life-changing. From dealing with symptoms to navigating treatment, managing medical problems is no easy feat.

And while accessibility upgrades and wellness integrations can certainly make a home more habitable in these instances, some people choose to pack up and move altogether—particularly celebrities.

Because their diagnoses may be complicated by the nuances that come along with fame and being in the public eye, it’s no surprise that some celebs may choose to find a home with more privacy when faced with health challenges.

Of course, celebrities may also have the means to relocate when particular symptoms could be managed more easily in a different climate.

Although some high profile individuals prefer to keep these kinds of decisions close to the chest, a handful of celebs have spoken candidly about the health-related circumstances that inspired them to migrate.

Recent findings suggest that jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg recently offloaded their longtime Illinois residence for $2.6 million. The transaction comes just as “The Masked Singer” host has publicly shared her experience dealing with the effects of “mold and mycotoxin poisoning.”.

According to recent reports, during the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” she revealed that she’s been living in a tent after undergoing the costly experience of remediating her home.

In a later episode, McCarthy also noted that she has discarded all of her clothing and furniture in a continued attempt to escape the mold.

In the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation.

“I’m so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” McCarthy remarked.

McCarthy and Wahlberg have yet to make a permanent move, but the sale of their St. Charles property could certainly be the first step towards change.

Retired Major League Baseball star Matt Holliday and his wife, Leslie Holliday, were left with no choice but to leave the dream home they’d built in Stillwater, OK, when he was diagnosed with a respiratory disease.

“The doctor mentioned he needed to get to dry climate quick,” listing agent Vincent Clark told the Phoenix Business Journal.

Clark is the agent representing the sale of the Paradise Valley, AZ property the Hollidays initially relocated to.

They purchased the $10.6 million home in February of this year after the World Series champion received the diagnosis a week after a water leak had affected their 136-acre custom home in Oklahoma, which is still on the market for $8.95 million.

While the sprawling Arizona property was well-equipped with “substantial healthy-home enhancements” including air and water filtration and conditioning systems, Clark revealed that the Hollidays are seeking a home with an existing guest house, although the 7,781-square-foot home they’re hoping to sell includes transferred approved aims for an 845-square-foot guest casita.

In an Aug.10 social media post, “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” alum Mikayla Matthews admitted that her “home situation is always up in the air.”.

The reality TV personality was diagnosed with Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CIRS), which she believes was triggered by extended exposure to mold-related toxins.

She and her family spent much of 2026 traveling in hopes of easing her symptoms, and temporarily relocated to Hawaii in May before heading to Florida in June in pursuit of a humid climate.

“The heavy metals in the air from Great Salt Lake drying up add to my toxic load everyday, so I can’t detox everything out,” she wrote in an Instagram post.

In October, Matthews revealed that her family was leaving the home she says was “making” her “sick,” and had purchased a fresh home in Utah, which is still under construction.

The “Tell It To My Heart” singer considered the move to be part of her healing process.

Dayne told People magazine that she’s feeling healthy four years after her diagnosis in July of this year.

“So far, so good,” she said of her health. “All clean.”.

In a recent development, “I feel disconnected, in the best way I’ve ever known,” she told People magazine. “It’s all about outdoors and nature which I really appreciate since I never had it growing up in New York and L.A.”.

Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different.
  • It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.
  • In a recent development, the tech giant said today that customers can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:36 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

According to recent reports, rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

In a recent development, the tech giant said today that customers can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

It has been revealed that however, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant people first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

Sources indicate that anthropic said people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the company said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s new “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

In a video posted on X, Anthropic revealed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Sources indicate that ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq.

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026.

It has been revealed that because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to people, Anthropic said.

As an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic said. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

There is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”.

According to recent reports, that could be a pretty substantial downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

#110665. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs
