Blockstream CEO Adam Back has explained the overnight sell-off on Kraken's Canadian-dollar markets that sent the exchange's BTC/CAD pair to C$24,250, or roughly $17,000, on Saturday morning, and stated that the drop started with the exchange's local USD/CAD market maker.

The Blockstream CEO addressed the issue on X on Saturday in a reply to a post that tracked large sell orders hitting Kraken's BTC/CAD order book at regular intervals throughout the night.

The $17,000 figure is based on the Bank of Canada's Friday rate of C$1.4325 per U.S. dollar. Kraken's BTC/CAD pair printed the C$24,250 low on Saturday morning, according to TradingView data.

"No, the reason was USDCAD Kraken local spot FX market-maker ran out of money, as it has depegged away from market rate 1.434," Back replied.

In the same post, the Blockstream CEO noted that it was "more accurate to say you could buy CAD discounted.".

Later, another X user argued that the Canadian dollar was in fact overvalued on Kraken during the sell-off, since anyone who held CAD could buy anything at a discount. Back agreed with the correction.

According to recent reports, "You are right. BTCUSD normal price, USDCAD CAD mispriced, like a shortage of CAD bid the price up," Back wrote.

On Sunday, the Blockstream CEO described the whole chain of events in two more posts on X.

According to Back, if the USD/CAD market maker failed, there were few buyers of BTC in Canadian dollars, and so the BTC/CAD price fell. In his view, traders would normally close such a gap with an arbitrage trade "by selling USD to CAD to buy if it BTCCAD doesn't track BTCUSD.".

Back wrote that the drop "liquidated people" and triggered stop losses "based on a local false price.".

"And then USDCAD followed because you could buy BTC cheaply in CAD, so it became logical to buy CAD way over par to take that arb," he added.

The BTC/CAD pair recovered later on Saturday, and on Sunday, it traded at C$86,236 on Kraken, according to TradingView.

Kraken remarked in a statement that its Canadian-dollar trading pairs faced heavy selling pressure starting around 20:00 UTC on Friday, and prices on these pairs fell significantly below those on other markets.

According to recent reports, the Kraken sell-off started on the same day that Bitcoin dropped to $59,370, its lowest level since July 2, according to CoinGlass data. On Friday, CoinGlass also recorded $1.57 billion in liquidations across the crypto market over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of that amount.

Still, the exchange mentioned that every order was processed correctly and that its security teams found no evidence of a breach or compromised accounts.

"Executed trades stand," Kraken said.

Alchemi CEO Zvi Sacks calls Jocelyn Freimuth "an invaluable partner" to the South African pharmacy and recommends her "without hesitation.".

Recent findings suggest that NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zvi Sacks, CEO of Alchemi Compounding Pharmacy in Johannesburg, South Africa, has credited Jocelyn Freimuth, PharmD, MBA, BSN, BCSCP, CEO of Camino Compass, with supporting his team on formulation development and troubleshooting.

Medicines sold in South Africa generally must be registered with the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA), which must first be satisfied that each is safe, effective, and of good quality. Section 14(4) of the Medicines and Related Substances Act exempts medicines compounded for an individual patient, as a July analysis by Werksmans Attorneys outlines, leaving quality largely in the compounding pharmacist's hands. Sterile preparations raise the stakes, since most are injected or infused and leave no room for contamination.

Formulation development in sterile compounding means choosing the ingredients, concentrations, and containers that keep a preparation stable and sterile through its shelf life. Troubleshooting starts when something fails, from early degradation to a failed sterility test, and traces the problem back to its source in the process.

"Jocelyn's scientific depth and experience have been especially valuable in addressing the critical aspects of safety and sterility, which matter enormously in a sterile compounding environment," remarked Sacks.

In a recent development, "Compounding rules differ from one country to the next, but sterility does not," stated Freimuth. "A preparation has to be right before it reaches the patient, and that is the standard I work to with every pharmacy, in the United States or abroad.".

Recent findings suggest that alchemi is among the compounding pharmacies Freimuth supports outside the United States. Her international work also includes specialty pharmacy lectures at universities in Vietnam and a research presentation at the 25th Asian Conference on Clinical Pharmacy in Bangkok in July 2026.

It has been revealed that for Sacks, how she works matters just as much. "Jocelyn is always willing to help, and she does it in a friendly, kind and approachable way," he noted. "Her guidance is practical and reliable, and she makes complex problems feel manageable. We really enjoy working with her and would recommend her without hesitation.".

About Jocelyn Freimuth and Camino Compass.

It has been revealed that jocelyn Freimuth, PharmD, MBA, BSN, BCSCP, is a board-certified sterile compounding pharmacist and the Co-Founder and CEO of Camino Compass, a Nashville-based healthcare consulting and management firm. Drawing on more than 15 years across nursing, pharmacy, regulatory compliance, education, and healthcare executive leadership, she advises pharmacies, clinics, telehealth organizations, and medical providers in the United States and internationally. The firm's services include operational pharmacy support, regulatory compliance, accreditation support, healthcare education, startup and build-out consulting and team training. For more information, visit caminocompass.com or connect with her on LinkedIn.

About Alchemi Compounding Pharmacy.

Recent findings suggest that alchemi Compounding Pharmacy is based in Midrand, Johannesburg, in South Africa's Gauteng province. Led by CEO Zvi Sacks, the pharmacy prepares customized medications for medical practitioners, allied healthcare professionals, and their patients. For more information, visit alchemicompoundingpharmacy.co.za.

Recent findings suggest that in light of this, three amendments are racing against the 2026 calendar, with only a few votes left to reach a majority and enter the two-week activation period. These include SingleAssetVault, LendingProtocol and confidential transfers.

All three remain below the required validator approval threshold of over 80% support, making the final weeks of the year increasingly notable for their activation prospects.

With about five weeks left in 2026, activation remains possible this year, but additional validator support for each amendment must arrive soon enough and be sustained to complete the required two-week activation window.

Sources indicate that the lending protocol allows on-chain fixed-term, uncollateralized loans from pooled funds in a Single Asset Vault. There are two amendments: LendingProtocolV1_1 and the original Lending Protocol amendment.

In a recent development, the focus is on LendingProtocolV1_1, which extends the Lending Protocol and SingleAssetVault amendments with a newly introduced closed-ended vault and cash-basis accounting. With the amendment, new loan brokers can only be created against closed-ended vaults.

LendingProtocolV1_1 has reached 70.59% support with 24 out of 34 validators voting yes, according to XRPScan data. It needs 28 votes to reach a majority, or more than 80% of 34 votes, meaning it has just four votes left.

A major privacy amendment for the XRP Ledger, confidential transfers, has 64.71% support and 22 of 34 validators voting yes. Confidential transfers, which rely on advanced cryptography (EC-ElGamal and ZKPs), offer institutional-grade privacy for Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) and need six more yes votes to enter the activation window.

SingleAssetVault creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. It has gained 73.53% support so far with 25 out of 34 validators voting in favor. Reaching more than 80% of 34 votes requires 28 votes; thus, three votes remain for it to enter the activation window.

Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.
  • In a recent development, the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Latest Yorkers’ doors.
  • The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.

Amazon and Fresh York City are fighting again.

In a recent development, the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Latest Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Sources indicate that companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

According to recent reports, in a blog post, Amazon stated it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the manufacturer wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

Amazon rolled out its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

Industry observers note that in a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel remarked the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the manufacturer works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the tech giant abruptly canceled intends to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most Upcoming Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Latest Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6.

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Upcoming Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Recent findings suggest that amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company mentioned it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

15 contestants emerge from The Realm app to compete for $100,000 in a four-episode adventure series premiering Dec. 2, with Bass Pro Shops as official basecamp sponsor.

CHICAGO, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Minelab, the global leader in metal detecting technology, launches Race to the Realm Finals, an original YouTube competition series that showcases the skill, discovery, and adventure of metal detecting. The four-episode series premieres Wednesday, Dec. 2 on Minelab's YouTube channel with new episodes released every Wednesday through Dec. 23.

According to recent reports, the competition began in The Realm, Minelab's digital community mobile app, where metal detecting enthusiasts competed for a chance to become one of 15 finalists. Now, those contestants will face a series of challenges designed to test their technical skills, instincts, endurance, and ability to perform under pressure. At stake: a $100,000 grand prize and the title of Race to the Realm champion.

The series marks a newly introduced chapter in Minelab's investment in the metal detecting community, bringing the passion and expertise of everyday enthusiasts to the screen while introducing new audiences to the hobby.

Recent findings suggest that "Metal detecting has always been driven by curiosity, skill, and the thrill of what you might discover next," remarked Ben Harvey, president and executive general manager of Minelab. "Race to the Realm is an investment in the people who make this community extraordinary and in the future of the hobby itself. We're creating latest ways for enthusiasts to connect, challenge themselves, and share their passion, while showing a much broader audience how much adventure and skill metal detecting has to offer.".

From Digital Community to Real-World Competition.

Race to the Realm connects Minelab's digital community with a high-stakes, real-world adventure. Through The Realm app, participants engaged in a three-round national competition, earning points through digital challenges, community engagement, and real-world activities. Five competitors from each round advanced, securing their spots among the 15 final contestants.

Sources indicate that the original YouTube series takes that competition further with skills and adventure in the spotlight. Across four episodes, contestants must adapt to unfamiliar challenges, make strategic decisions, and put their detecting expertise to work as the stakes rise.

The series also gives viewers a closer look at metal detecting as an evolving, skill-based outdoor pursuit, combining technology, problem-solving, exploration, and the possibility of unexpected discovery.

Bass Pro Shops Joins as Official Basecamp Sponsor.

Bass Pro Shops, a leading national outdoor retailer, served as the official basecamp sponsor of Race to the Realm Finals, supporting the competition and connecting the series to the broader outdoor adventure community.

The partnership connects the series to the broader outdoor recreation community and reinforces Minelab's commitment to expanding the reach of metal detecting.

A New Chapter for the Metal Detecting Community.

Race to the Realm is part of Minelab's broader effort to build a more connected community and create latest opportunities for enthusiasts to share their passion.

According to recent reports, through The Realm app, users can connect with fellow detectorists, share finds and engage with the community. The app will also feature all four episodes of Race to the Realm Finals, along with exclusive finalist interviews and behind-the-scenes content that takes viewers deeper into the competition.

Together, the series and The Realm create newly introduced ways for longtime enthusiasts and newcomers to experience metal detecting.

It has been revealed that race to the Realm Finals premieres Dec. 2 on Minelab's official YouTube channel, with new episodes every Wednesday through Dec. 23.

Meet the 15 contestants, follow the competition, and watch the adventure unfold at the Race to the Realm Hub starting Dec. 2.

Headquartered in Mawson Lakes, South Australia, with regional offices in Ireland, India, UAE, Mexico, Brazil and the USA, Minelab develops and manufactures world-leading handheld detection systems for adventure, discovery, and safety.

Ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, Ripple USD (RLUSD), has now entered the top five stablecoins by market cap, reaching a newly introduced all-time high in its circulating supply, a major milestone for the stablecoin less than two years after its launch. RLUSD went live in December 2024.

RLUSD has surpassed World Liberty Financial USD (USD1), Global Dollar (USDG) and PayPal USD (PYUSD) to become the fifth-largest stablecoin in the world, according to data from CoinMarketCap. Only Tether’s USDT, Circle’s USDC, Ethena’s USDe, and Dai (DAI) are ahead of it.

The milestone is proof of the rapid growth RLUSD has experienced in a competitive stablecoin market dominated by established players like Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC.

RLUSD’s total circulating supply across the XRP Ledger and Ethereum has reached a fresh high, with $2.85 billion in circulation, according to Ripple’s stablecoin tracker.

Industry observers note that ethereum commands $2.089 billion of this total figure, while $768 million in supply sits on the XRP Ledger. While Ethereum currently holds the larger share of RLUSD’s supply, XRPL has seen significant activity in RLUSD settlement volumes.

In March 2025, during a Bloomberg TV interview, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse projected that RLUSD would enter the top five stablecoins; that projection has now been fulfilled.

According to RWA Foundation, Ripple led weekly stablecoin growth, adding $75.4 million in the last seven days. This growth was reflected in RLUSD's market cap, allowing it to surpass World Liberty Financial USD to clinch the fifth spot in global stablecoin rankings.

Former Ripple executive Anthony Welfare highlighted this growth in a recent X post, saying, “RLUSD is the only major stablecoin growing right now.”.

Welfare noted that RLUSD supply is up nearly 20% in three weeks, rising from $2.42 billion to $2.9 billion, while USDT has fallen by $5 billion and USDC by $3 billion over the same period.

The XRP Ledger accounts for the majority of RLUSD settlements: in an analogy on X, Welfare noted that XRPL holds about 27% of RLUSD’s supply but processed 57% of its volume last week, amounting to $6.7 billion versus Ethereum, which recorded $5 billion.

  • On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still indicates Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.
  • Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still indicates Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Sources indicate that most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It notes: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

It has been revealed that the schedule is fixed. Circle confirmed in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no newly introduced burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the tech giant wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

The main text above it claims something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Industry observers note that circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle stated "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

It has been revealed that the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

In a recent development, for Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:56 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante noted. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”.

Industry observers note that during the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:.

Industry observers note that the commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

According to recent reports, “Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”.

Sources indicate that memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”.

According to recent reports, for AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

According to recent reports, “We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:.

Sources indicate that protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”.

Recent findings suggest that at Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production problems, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

In a recent development, “If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti stated during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very crucial metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”.

Industry observers note that for International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

Sources indicate that “This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:.

Industry observers note that for organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

Recent findings suggest that “We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely rapidly,” Ernst noted during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:.

In a recent development, walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”.

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has declared a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the firm’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

In a recent development, the newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, noted today in a news release.

Industry observers note that “By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith noted. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”.

It has been revealed that mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the firm’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

Sources indicate that bitcoin (BTC) fell as low as $55,081 on Nov. 21, its lowest price since September 2024, according to TradingView data. The cryptocurrency then bounced back and was trading at $60,583 on Sunday, after it opened November at $77,425.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin has lost 21.6% so far in November 2026, according to CryptoRank. The last time Bitcoin had a worse month was June 2022, when the cryptocurrency lost 37.9%, according to the same data.

In a recent development, the four-year cycle theory ties Bitcoin's market cycles to halvings, and its supporters point to 2014, 2018 and 2022 as the years when each bear market went through its final sell-off. In this context, 2026 is the next year in that row, and the next Bitcoin halving is expected in April 2028. The previous three halvings took place in July 2016, May 2020 and April 2024.

In a recent development, bitcoin set its record above $1,100 in late 2013. In February 2014, the Japanese exchange Mt. Gox, which handled most Bitcoin trading in 2013, filed for bankruptcy after it lost about 850,000 BTC. In November 2014, Bitcoin gained 11.6%, according to CryptoRank, but December of that year brought a 15.3% drop, and the bottom below $200 came in January 2015.

In December 2017, Bitcoin reached a record near $20,000 on the back of the ICO boom, and during 2018, the ICO market dried up. In November 2018, the crypto market crashed after the Bitcoin Cash hard fork and the so-called hash war between the two camps of miners, and Bitcoin lost 36.4% that month. The cryptocurrency then lost another 6.4% in December 2018 and set its cycle low at about $3,200 in the middle of that month.

The 2021 record near $69,000 came in November 2021. In May 2022, the Terra ecosystem collapsed, and in July of that year, Celsius and Three Arrows Capital filed for bankruptcy. In November of that year, the FTX exchange went bankrupt. Bitcoin lost 16.1% in November 2022 and set its bear market bottom at around $15,500 on Nov. 21, 2022, four years to the day before the latest low. December of that year brought a 3.7% loss, and in January 2023, Bitcoin gained 39.9%.

In the current cycle, Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025. In 2026, Bitcoin has lost value in six of the 11 months so far, according to CryptoRank. On Nov. 20, the cryptocurrency fell below $60,000 for the first time since July, and the decline continued the next day.

The latest drop comes amid a broad sell-off on Wall Street, where technology and AI stocks came under pressure, and amid expectations of further interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

SPCX stock since its IPO: a $225.64 peak, a $104.83 low and a Dec. 8 unlock

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX's SPCX stock closed day one at $160.95, hit $225.64, fell to $104.83 and faces a Dec.
  • It has been revealed that few investors could buy into SpaceX when it began trading, because the company held back almost all of its shares from the market.
  • Different forces have set the price at different times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX's SPCX stock closed day one at $160.95, hit $225.64, fell to $104.83 and faces a Dec. 8 lockup expiry. Here are 3 key numbers.

It has been revealed that few investors could buy into SpaceX when it began trading, because the company held back almost all of its shares from the market. That left a small pool of stock, and a modest number of buyers or sellers could move its price sharply. Investors have pushed SPCX through wide swings in its short public life for that reason. Those swings reveal as much about how many shares could trade as about what the rocket business is worth.

Different forces have set the price at different times. Buyers drove it up on the first day. A stock with so few shares in circulation can also move on bets against it and on changes in how many shares are free to trade. Those forces come from the mechanics of trading rather than from anyone's judgment of the manufacturer, so no price at any one moment settles what SpaceX is worth. A shareholder, or someone thinking of buying, has to decide which number to treat as the reference point: the offer price, the debut, the peak, the low or today's price. Each choice gives a different answer to whether SPCX has rewarded its investors.

Investing.com tracks SPCX's trading history, price extremes and share supply since its June 2026 listing. That record covers the stock's whole public life rather than a verdict from any single day, starting from a float of under 5% of shares when trading opened. It takes in the large blocks of stock still waiting for release, the sharp distance between the stock's best and worst days, and the debut that set the starting line for everything after it. Taken together, those numbers describe a stock whose price investors are still working out, not one they have agreed on.

Sources indicate that spaceX's first day of trading gave investors who bought at the offer price a clear win, and that gain became the reference point for every move since. Buyers who paid the $135 offer price ended the session holding shares worth $160.95, according to Investing.com. Buyers were even more eager during the day than that close suggests. Shares reached $176.52 at their high for the day, CNBC reports, and the stock finished the session below that level. The closing price marked where enthusiasm had cooled, not where it peaked. Any later gain or loss measured from it starts at a level traders had already retreated from once.

Not everyone agreed that SpaceX was worth even the offer price. Keith Snyder, senior analyst at CFRA Research, gave the stock a sell rating and a $115 12-month target, according to CNBC. In his view, the price was too high before buyers added any first-day premium. "It was a hard pill to swallow even there," Snyder stated of the $135 pricing. The debut showed how much buyers wanted the shares. It did not settle whether SpaceX was worth what they paid.

Credit: Mariia Berezovsky / Unsplash.

Recent findings suggest that investors who bought SpaceX shares at the IPO price and held them are losing money, with the stock priced 11.47% below the offer in late November, according to Investing.com. That price was recorded in the middle of the Nov. 25 session, not at the close, so it is a snapshot of one afternoon, not a floor or a final verdict on SpaceX.

In a recent development, the distance between the stock's best and worst days is wide enough that no single price explains much on its own. Buyers pushed SPCX to its all-time high of $225.64 on June 16, in its first days of trading, so the top was set in the debut rush and not after a long run of gains. The low of $104.83 came on Aug. 3, early in a month when many investors were betting against the stock. Short interest peaked at 34% of public shares in the week before Aug. 12, according to S3 Partners figures reported by . A low set during a stretch of heavy short bets may reflect investor mood that summer more than what the company is worth.

Industry observers note that the opening was also a managed event. CNBC reports that Nasdaq $NDAQ President Nelson Griggs saw strong backing among the orders for the opening, and that Morgan Stanley $MS led the effort to stabilize the stock's price. With a bank assigned to that role, the debut came out of an organized offering as well as open trading, and later sessions would show what price buyers set on their own.

The debut set a starting point, not a minimum price, and the months that followed would test how much of it held.

Industry observers note that short sellers pulled back sharply as the stock climbed off its bottom. By Aug. 12, short interest had fallen to about 11% of public shares, CNBC reports from S3 Partners figures, a drop that came partly from the larger pool of tradable shares after the first lockup expired the week before. "Shorts that wanted to short are out of bullets," said Ihor Dusaniwsky, managing director of predictive analytics at S3 Partners. With short interest down sharply, support for the price depends on investors who want to own SPCX.

SPCX's range records how investors were positioned as much as what SpaceX is worth.

Credit: Markus Winkler / Unsplash.

The next massive influence on SPCX's price may be a date on the calendar rather than news from a launch pad. On Dec. 8, the final IPO lockup tranche expires, and up to 797.6 million more shares become eligible for sale, according to Investing.com. That puts a large fresh group of potential sellers in the market on a single day. Some early holders have had the right to sell since the first lockup expired on Aug. 6, CNBC reports, and December adds to stock that has already been changing hands. To judge what December could mean for the price, investors first need to see how much new stock they have already had to take on.

The supply of tradable SPCX shares has grown in large steps more than once since the June debut. The August release alone made 911 million shares eligible for sale. CNBC reports that SpaceX sold 639 million shares when it listed, and further batches became eligible on Aug. 20, in September and in October. Investors have therefore already absorbed a single release larger than the entire IPO. December is best read as the last of the IPO-era unlocks rather than a single sudden event.

According to recent reports, shares that become eligible in December may push the price down, but nobody is required to sell them. "While the step-up in potential supply is meaningful, we think investors should understand that shares becoming eligible for sale does not mean the full tranche will be offered into the market," Mizuho analysts remarked in a report, as reported by CNBC. The largest block of stock is not part of the December release at all. Elon Musk holds more than 6 billion SpaceX shares and cannot sell them until his lockup ends in June 2027, according to CNBC. Through December, any selling from the lockup releases comes from early investors rather than the organization's largest holder.

For anyone holding or eyeing SPCX, two questions remain open: how much early investors actually sell, and what Musk does once his own lockup ends.

  • The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am.

Industry observers note that orchard Robotics, an agtech manufacturer using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was revealed Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, stated in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Industry observers note that FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XTI Aerospace, Inc. (Nasdaq: XTIA) ("XTI Aerospace," "XTI," or the "Manufacturer"), parent company of Drone Nerds, LLC, ("Drone Nerds"), a leading drone solutions platform serving commercial, enterprise and government customers, today announced that the Company has eliminated all outstanding Class B Units held by the sellers of Drone Nerds. In addition, the Company has entered into warrant exchange agreements, subject to customary closing conditions, with holders representing approximately 40% of its outstanding warrants, simplifying the Company's capital structure.

Sources indicate that in a transaction dated November 18, 2026, all Class B Units of XTI Drones Holdings, LLC, a subsidiary formed in connection with XTI Aerospace's November 2025 acquisitions of Drone Nerds and Anzu Robotics, were converted into 6,524,576 shares of XTI Aerospace common stock. They were exchanged on a one-to-one basis. These securities are held directly by The Origin Group DN, Inc. and The Origin Group AZ, Inc. Following the exchange, no Class B Units remain outstanding.

Sources indicate that the Firm also declared today that it has entered into Securities Exchange Agreements with certain holders of outstanding warrants to purchase shares of the Company's common stock, par value $0.001 per share (the "Common Stock"). Pursuant to the Exchange Agreements, certain warrant holders agreed to exchange warrants exercisable for an aggregate of 8,522,052 shares of Common Stock for an aggregate of 2,840,690 newly issued shares of Common Stock. Following the Exchange, warrants to purchase approximately 12,670,129 shares of Common Stock remain outstanding.

The warrants were originally issued pursuant to the Underwriting Agreement dated June 24, 2025 between the Company and ThinkEquity LLC as representative of the several underwriters named therein, and the Placement Agency Agreement dated September 12, 2025 between the Company and ThinkEquity, and certain warrants were issued to ThinkEquity and its designees in connection with certain financings.

As a result of these transactions, XTI Aerospace now has approximately 47.8 million shares of common stock as of November 25, 2026.

Sources indicate that "The elimination of certain legacy acquisition and financing securities marks an crucial step in simplifying our capital structure," noted Jeremy Schneiderman, Interim CEO of XTI Aerospace. "With the removal of the Class B Units we believe we are better positioned with a solid foundation to execute on our strategic growth initiatives while enhancing shareholder value.".

ThinkEquity served as financial advisor, and Blank Rome LLP and Taft Law served as legal counsel in connection with the transactions.

It has been revealed that XTI Aerospace, Inc. ("XTI") (Nasdaq: XTIA) is focused on building a leading platform for commercial and government drone adoption in the growing unmanned aircraft systems ("UAS") industry. Through its subsidiary, Drone Nerds, LLC, XTI supports enterprise and government customers in sectors including public safety, agriculture, construction, and energy across the drone program lifecycle, from hardware sourcing and deployment to training, service, repair, and the proprietary Always Flyingâ¢ program. Its established U.S. customer base and reputation as a trusted solutions provider position the company as a go-to-market partner for drone manufacturers and software developers seeking to scale in the domestic market.

For more information about XTI, please visit xtiaerospace.com and follow XTI on LinkedIn, Instagram, X, and YouTube.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Famous Bitcoin (BTC) advocate and investor Bill Miller IV mentioned that it is much easier to value the world's largest cryptocurrency than AI investments, even though Bitcoin does not produce any cash flow.
  • He said that this has to do with the expectations investors have when it comes to these two assets, specifically regarding their capacity to deliver future profits.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous Bitcoin (BTC) advocate and investor Bill Miller IV mentioned that it is much easier to value the world's largest cryptocurrency than AI investments, even though Bitcoin does not produce any cash flow.

He said that this has to do with the expectations investors have when it comes to these two assets, specifically regarding their capacity to deliver future profits.

In a recent X post, Miller, who is the chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, broke down why he thinks that it's easier to make an investment case for Bitcoin than for AI companies.

In a recent development, "Bitcoin and AI owners have different expectations. The owners of AI expect companies will one day produce free cash flow. Bitcoin owners never did or will expect this," Miller said.

And the end result is that "the valuation case is still much easier for Bitcoin than AI.".

Simply put, when investors buy stocks in AI companies, there is an expectation that at some point these companies will deliver big profits and free cash flow.

Free cash flow is the money a organization produces from its operations after capital expenditures. This is a significant metric for understanding the value of a company.

However, when it comes to AI companies, it can be difficult to assign a value because investors need to try to determine what kind of revenue these companies will generate, how much they will invest in infrastructure, and when these investments will start to deliver sufficient returns.

Miller has made it a point to push back against the argument that Bitcoin does not have value because it doesn't produce cash flow.

In a commentary from June 30, Miller explained that the traditional way of looking at intrinsic value, which revolves around future cash flows, doesn't really capture the potential of Bitcoin as a decentralized monetary network.

Instead, Miller said that Bitcoin's value could be determined by comparing its potential role within the global financial system to that of gold.

In his view, Bitcoin could theoretically reach about $1.4 million per coin if it achieved a valuation similar to gold's. At least, that's what he calculated at the time.

S&P Global $SPGI Ratings is weighing a one-notch downgrade of Nvidia $NVDA's credit rating, pointing to unease over how the chipmaker is managed and governed after CEO Jensen Huang's exit and subsequent comeback, according to Bloomberg.

The rating agency said Nvidia's AA grade, which is the third-highest tier, could be lowered once a 90-day review ends, a process that puts the company on CreditWatch with negative implications, according to Bloomberg.

"We expect the potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations or disclosures lead us to believe Nvidia's reputation or future business prospects have been harmed," S&P said in a statement on Wednesday, according to Bloomberg.

According to recent reports, nvidia's board brought Huang back as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after he stepped down following reports of two extramarital affairs. One of the relationships was with a woman suspected of spying for China. Alice Huang, who has no family relationship to Jensen Huang, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer.

Industry observers note that nvidia mentioned in a statement that its board "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and is confident the reinstatement "poses no national security risk." The board had opened an independent investigation earlier this month after Jensen Huang disclosed the affair to employees. The board said nothing it has seen suggests Nvidia's trade secrets or U.S. national security were put at risk.

The Justice and Commerce departments mentioned on Nov. 17 that they were looking into whether Megaspeed redirected Nvidia chips in breach of American export rules.

Several Republican lawmakers have criticized the reinstatement and mentioned they would seek answers. Jensen Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter have confirmed they will appear for transcribed interviews with House committees on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2. The Senate Banking Committee has revealed a public hearing with Huang on Dec. 3.

Industry News: StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.
  • In a recent development, stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft.
  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

In a recent development, stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup declared a upcoming round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

Recent findings suggest that stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer noted an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has stated the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

According to recent reports, it also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor stated up to 5,000 owners may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity notes it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

Recent findings suggest that how it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the tech giant says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

According to recent reports, stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-latest releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

It has been revealed that stepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

Industry observers note that the firm has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

Industry observers note that what’s next: StepSecurity aims to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The organization claims it also prepares to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

Tech Report: Trump’s Nvidia intervention is the reverse of how Bush handled Enron’s Ken Lay

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that once upon a time, a hugely valuable manufacturer sat at the cutting edge of an industry the whole economy depended on, and it had close ties to the White House.
  • It has been revealed that that was Enron in 2001, and President George W.
  • “I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that once upon a time, a hugely valuable manufacturer sat at the cutting edge of an industry the whole economy depended on, and it had close ties to the White House. Then came signs of financial irregularities on a scandalous scale.

It has been revealed that that was Enron in 2001, and President George W. Bush stood back and let justice take its course. On Monday, President Donald Trump did the reverse with Nvidia: the chipmaker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after he resigned over reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese national U.S. officials suspect of spying and who is no relation.

“I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview. Huang has denied compromising national security, and no one has charged him with a crime.

Sources indicate that nvidia and Enron are not like-for-like scandals, although some commentators see the connection; the details so far are scandalous but are not Enron-style accounting fraud. Still, with some financial commentators fearing an AI bubble could pop and trigger the next financial crisis, Kenneth “Kenny Boy” Lay’s case is instructive. It reveals how far Washington has moved from treating major companies as targets to treating them as partners.

Industry observers note that lay was a fixture of Houston’s energy establishment, and his ties to the Bush family went back to the first President Bush. Bush adviser Karl Rove later called any idea that Lay was a “close intimate” of Bush “ludicrous,” but they were close enough that Bush gave him the “Kenny Boy” nickname.

The money was never in doubt. Across Bush’s political career, Enron, its employees and their families gave him more than $550,000, more than any other single source, and Lay was his biggest financial backer.

As Texas governor, Bush signed a 1999 electricity deregulation law that opened new markets to Enron. During the 2000 campaign, he traveled to Houston for the Astros’ first game at Enron Field, where Lay threw out the first pitch.

According to recent reports, wall Street loved the company, too. Fortune named Enron America’s most innovative company six years running, even as Fortune’s Bethany McLean became the first major business journalist to ask, in March 2001, how exactly Enron made its money.

When Enron was collapsing in October 2001, Lay phoned Treasury Secretary Paul O’Neill and Commerce Secretary Donald Evans. Both said they did nothing to help. Nearly five years later, with Bush still in the White House, a jury convicted Lay and former CEO Jeffrey Skilling of fraud.

Skilling’s 24-year sentence was among the longest ever handed to a corporate executive; a judge cut it to 14 years in 2013. Former CFO Andrew Fastow got six years and was released after about five. Lay died before he could be sentenced, and his convictions were vacated.

The two companies already share a footnote. At the end of November 2001, days before Enron filed for bankruptcy, Standard & Poor’s dropped it from the S&P 500 and replaced it with a Santa Clara graphics-chip maker called Nvidia.

Sources indicate that huang’s closeness to Trump is newer, and he built it deliberately. CNBC reports that Huang spent two years cultivating an “unparalleled relationship” with Trump while Nvidia lobbied for looser limits on selling advanced chips to China.

It has been revealed that nvidia gave $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and $25 million to his White House ballroom, and it initially sought to keep the ballroom gift anonymous. In April 2025, Huang attended a $1-million-a-head dinner at Mar-a-Lago, after which the administration briefly held off on restricting Nvidia’s H20 chips before imposing the limits days later.

In a recent development, by July, the administration had reversed course and begun approving sales to China, and in December Trump remarked Nvidia could sell its more powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers. Democrats, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, have tied the donations to those decisions, but there is no known hard evidence of any specific quid pro quo — something that could change under the incoming, heavily Democratic Congress.

Industry observers note that nvidia shares closed up about 31.5% on Monday, their best day since 2003, adding $952 billion in market value, and the S&P 500 rose 4.73%. The rebound reversed much of the slide that followed Huang’s exit, although the stock gave back single-digit percentages on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The stakes are hard to overstate. Nvidia ranks No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list to top $4 trillion in market value.

Sources indicate that trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his Office of Government Ethics filings, and CBS News estimated his stake gained between $1.3 million and $14.8 million on Monday. The White House told CBS that independent managers run his portfolio.

Nvidia matters well beyond the president’s portfolio. The manufacturer, and Huang personally, have been called “the central bank of AI,” a label The Economist applied after tallying more than $70 billion in Nvidia investments in startups over three years and $300 billion in financial support to customers.

It has been revealed that owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management who writes the Owenomics newsletter, says that label carries a curse. In his telling, once an entity is called “the central bank of” its field, it becomes “a prime candidate for a cosmic smackdown.”.

Long-Term Capital Management, called “the central bank of volatility” before its 1998 collapse, was the first victim he knows of. FTX, called “the central bank of crypto” six months before Sam Bankman-Fried’s arrest, was the second.

It has been revealed that the Economist has also compared Nvidia’s financing to the vendor lending Cisco and Lucent did in the dot-com boom. Cisco is the other fallen high-flier Nvidia is most often measured against, usually by outlier voices; it is the favorite comparison of “Significant Short” trader Michael Burry, who has become a Substack star during the AI boom.

In a recent development, the Enron prosecutions marked the end of an era. In “The Chickenshit Club,” ProPublica’s Jesse Eisinger holds up a Justice Department that set up a dedicated task force, charged nearly all of Enron’s top executives and did so against a friend of the president. He argues that the department has since lost the will and ability to prosecute top executives.

The title comes from James Comey, who led the FBI’s 2016 investigation of Hillary Clinton’s emails and is now fighting a third attempt by Trump’s Justice Department to prosecute him. As U.S. attorney in Manhattan, Comey told prosecutors who had never lost a trial that they belonged to the “Chickenshit Club,” meaning they were too cautious to take on hard cases.

After the financial crisis, a University of Chicago Law Review article noted that Kareem Serageldin, a Credit Suisse banker sentenced to 30 months, was the only banker jailed in the U.S. for a role in the crash. In 2013, Attorney General Eric Holder told the Senate that the size of some banks had “an inhibiting impact” on prosecutions; he later said banks were not too significant to jail.

It has been revealed that in Eisinger’s telling, that retreat left prosecutors unwilling to pursue big-company executives. Trump has now gone further, treating companies less as targets than as partners.

Recent findings suggest that he has used the pardon power liberally in both terms. He pardoned Nikola founder Trevor Milton, who had been sentenced to four years for securities and wire fraud, and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao in October 2025. A not-yet-published study reported by Law360 found that 49 of Trump’s 89 pardons unrelated to Jan. 6 or the fake-elector scheme went to white-collar defendants.

In a recent development, his administration has also taken a 10% stake in Intel, a golden share in U.S. Steel and a 15% cut of Nvidia and AMD chip sales to China. Foreign Policy describes it as state capitalism of a kind few predecessors embraced.

Nvidia now sits in that firm. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that Trump and Vice President JD Vance were briefed and saw no evidence Huang did anything illegal. Attorney General Todd Blanche publicly called Nvidia “a good corporate citizen” but declined to say whether investigators had examined Huang.

Industry observers note that other probes continue. The Securities and Exchange Commission is conducting a civil investigation of Nvidia, The Wall Street Journal has reported, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has subpoenaed the manufacturer.

Whether this becomes a political scandal is unsettled. AI skeptic Gary Marcus asked in his Substack newsletter this week whether “Jensengate” could take down the president, writing that “you can bet your last dollar the incoming Congress is going to take an interest.”.

Sources indicate that when Enron collapsed, Lay called two members of Bush’s Cabinet, and both noted they did nothing to help. When Nvidia’s chief executive was ousted, Trump openly said he brokered the deal to bring him back.

“I didn’t use the word ‘prosecuted,’” Trump told CNBC. “I said that we believe he’s fine. He’s absolutely fine. I gave them enough assurance.”.

It has been revealed that the next test comes Dec. 3, when Huang is scheduled to appear at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing. The Enron precedent suggests why lawmakers may keep pressing: it took years and a dedicated task force for Bush’s Justice Department to finish.
