Industry News: How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • It has been revealed that it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • Sources indicate that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

It has been revealed that it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Sources indicate that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous enhancement that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

According to recent reports, no. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the firm has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella stated, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Industry observers note that some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

It has been revealed that MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

Industry observers note that MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

In a recent development, full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in significant, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

Industry observers note that what happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the organization with reports.

Industry observers note that the first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

According to recent reports, no surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

In a recent development, meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple customers to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

According to recent reports, more broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

It has been revealed that OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

It has been revealed that nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he stated, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Industry observers note that think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

According to recent reports, it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

According to recent reports, proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It reveals how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository states a yes vote does two things:.

It has been revealed that it also states plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

A no vote would stop the whole blueprint. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 demonstrated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

According to recent reports, turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Industry observers note that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

It has been revealed that the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Sources indicate that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

Sources indicate that at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Sources indicate that proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

Sources indicate that so Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the proposal goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

UPDATED 16:15 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker this past Monday.

According to recent reports, nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: its share price closed 3.8% lower.

It has been revealed that other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.56% and 0.57%, respectively.

The semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.77% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The company missed expectations across the board. Ambarella remarked that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the firm has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Sources indicate that companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.75% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

According to recent reports, in contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3.12% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2.02%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an important AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: it’s down 5.09% from yesterday.

It has been revealed that anthropic ended the trading session with a 1.08% gain. The firm thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq gained 0.61% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

Renowned financial guru and Rich Dad Poor Dad author Robert Kiyosaki has offered compelling insight into the reasons behind his buying spree of Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH) despite the current crypto market crash.

Kiyosaki, who is an esteemed investor, predicts that a financial crisis could be on the horizon, and it might be even worse than the 2008 market crash. He believes that crypto assets and other hard assets are an effective hedge against the repercussions of government-induced overborrowing and money printing.

The financial guru's latest X post explains his rationale behind investing in Bitcoin, Ethereum, gold, silver, real estate, and oil instead of traditional financial assets.

"Why I am buying real (no ETFs) gold, silver, Bitcoin, and Ethereum," Kiyosaki noted in his latest post.

He attributed his views to the Federal Reserve, the U.S. Treasury and the colossal debt obligations of the U.S.

Industry observers note that according to Kiyosaki, the government's inability to curb spending will lead to massive money printing in the future. This might erode the purchasing power of the U.S. dollar.

"The BIG PRINT is about to begin," Kiyosaki warned.

This is the core reason for his investments in Bitcoin and Ethereum. He believes that these assets will rise in value when the government is forced to aggressively print money in response to escalating financial problems.

Sources indicate that moreover, he believes that holding these crypto assets directly would be better than investing in exchange-traded funds (ETFs). However, he did not offer a reason for his opposition to ETFs in his post.

Furthermore, Kiyosaki stated that the next financial crisis could be much bigger than the global financial crisis of 2008.

"This crash we are just now sliding into is much bigger than 2008. Possibly a global depression," he commented.

He also mentioned that his gold, silver, Bitcoin and Ethereum holdings could make him one of the ultra-rich if his predictions come true.

Recent findings suggest that however, Kiyosaki mentioned some figures that were not entirely accurate. For instance, he stated that the U.S. national debt stood at $49 trillion. But according to Treasury data, the national debt was about $40.7 trillion in November 2026. Also, his claim that the U.S. is printing $1 trillion every 90 days conflates government debt with money printing.

Although Kiyosaki is a strong believer in Bitcoin, he recently advised investors not to buy Bitcoin immediately amid the digital asset's current price slump.

On Nov. 20, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author cautioned against catching a 'falling knife.'.

"Never grab a falling knife." This means that investors should wait for the market crash to end before buying.

"I started buying bitcoin around $20k after the market crashed last time," Kiyosaki recalled.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," he added.

CNBC's monthly record demonstrates core PCE inflation at 3.0% or higher from January through October 2026, with headline at 3.8% in October.

The inflation problem that defined 2026 was already in place when the year began, before any spring jump in food or energy prices. In January, core prices, which leave out food and energy, were up 3.1% from a year earlier, according to CNBC. The BEA reports that the full basket of consumer prices, food and fuel included, was up a smaller 2.8%. The pressure came from the everyday goods and services that make up most of a household budget rather than from the grocery aisle or the gas pump. Cheaper gas or groceries could not bring the rate down, because they were not what was pushing it up. Whatever happened to food and energy later in the year happened on top of a base that was already too high.

Households had more real income in January, but they bought only a little more with it. The BEA reports that real disposable income, meaning income after taxes and inflation, rose 0.7% in the month, while consumer spending grew just 0.1% once price increases are taken out. For that one month, income outpaced prices, and households had more real money to spend even as their carts held little more than before. Higher income helped families keep up, but it did nothing to lower the prices underneath it. The core rate that set the year's starting point remained in place.

February's inflation came from the everyday core of household budgets, not from the gas pump or the grocery store. The full price index climbed 0.4% over January, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data reported by CNBC, and the BEA reports the same monthly gain for the core measure, which sets food and energy aside. Leaving out the most volatile items removes none of the month's increase. Food and fuel prices tend to jump and then settle back, but pressure that runs through the rest of the household budget does not fade on its own.

Sources indicate that households paid for that broad rise by spending more money on barely more goods. Consumer spending rose 0.5% in dollars in February, according to the BEA, but it grew just 0.1% once higher prices are taken out. Almost all of the extra money went to cover price increases, and people came home with close to what they had bought in January. Their buying power shrank at the same time. Disposable income after taxes and inflation fell 0.5% for the month, so households kept up their spending on a smaller real income. Steady spending on falling real income leaves a gap that families have to cover somewhere.

The spring's jumps in food and fuel prices had become, by April, the level households were living with rather than one-off shocks. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, ran 3.3% above a year earlier, according to CNBC. BEA reports the same rate in its first estimate of the month, so there is little doubt about where the underlying base stood. In that same estimate, the full price index was up 3.8%. Core leaves out only food and energy, so the gap means households paid extra for groceries and fuel on top of a base that would not come down. They faced pressure from two directions at once: a stubborn base, and a costlier layer of essentials above it.

Prices that high left households with less buying power, and the loss held up when the figures were revisited. Real disposable income, meaning take-home pay after taxes and inflation, fell 0.5% in April, BEA reports, and BEA highlights the same drop in its May release. At first glance, that looks like a budget under strain from both sides, with prices rising while income went nowhere. Total personal income did not grow at all in April, but the weakness came from falling income for farm owners rather than from paychecks across the workforce. The income dip is more likely a one-off than a sign that jobs or wages were weakening. The lasting problem was prices.

June brought a monthly drop in prices but little relief for households. Prices slipped 0.1% from May, according to the first estimate from the BEA. Over 12 months, though, prices were still up 3.5%, according to CNBC. One cheaper month did little to undo a year of increases. For a family, June's bills stayed well above those of the previous summer, even though they stopped rising for a moment.

The first count made June look hotter than the later figures do. In its first estimate of the month, released July 30, 2026, the BEA puts the annual rate at 3.7%, a figure it later replaced. Neither reading comes close to the pace policymakers want. The open question is how much prices eased over the summer, not whether inflation was beaten.

The June drop most likely came from food and energy rather than from underlying prices. The BEA reports that in the same first estimate, core prices, which leave out food and energy, still rose 0.1% while the headline index fell. Underlying inflation did not pause in June. Cheaper groceries and fuel offset it for a single month, and the stubborn base underneath kept rising.

By late summer, households got a break from rising underlying prices, but the break only returned them to where the year began. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, were 3.0% higher in August than a year earlier, according to CNBC. That cooled rate held until inflation picked up again in the fall. Core inflation had already sat at that same low in winter, so households ended the summer no better off on underlying prices than they had been in February. A lull that puts prices back at the starting line is a pause, not progress.

The overall cost of living stayed higher than the core reading suggests. With food and fuel included, everything households bought cost 3.4% more than a year earlier, still above the cooled underlying rate. Prices also went on rising during the quiet month, up 0.3% from July, and BEA reports the same monthly increase in its own count. Even in the calmest stretch of 2026, households paid more.

Inflation was still running hot in October, the most recent month with data. Everything households bought cost 3.8% more than a year earlier, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis figures reported by CNBC. That pace is far from what the Federal Reserve aims for. Setting aside food and energy offers little comfort, because core prices were up 3.3% over the same 12 months, and the underlying rate had climbed back up after its cooler stretch in the summer. With the full measure above the core, food and energy added pressure on top of an already high base rather than causing the problem on their own.

October itself brought no pause. Overall prices rose 0.3% within the month, and core prices climbed at the same pace even with food and energy left out. For households, the squeeze did not ease as the year drew toward its close, and the goods and services they buy became more expensive again.

Industry observers note that americans kept spending through 2026, and a year of steady shopping can look like a sign that households were doing well. Their savings show something else. Americans set aside 4.5% of their after-tax income in January, according to the BEA, which was a modest margin even before the year's price increases set in. The BEA reports that the share was down to 2.6% in April, which left families that month with far less money put away for a lost job or an unexpected bill. Stubborn inflation can show up in a household budget this way. People keep buying what they need, and a smaller share of what they earn goes into savings.

Sources indicate that the strain on household budgets came from prices that stayed high all year, not from one bad month. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, tracks that underlying pressure. Even in February, one of the months when core inflation ran at its lowest of the year, core prices were up 3.0% from a year earlier, according to the BEA. The best months still left everyday goods and services costing noticeably more than they had the year before. Food and energy prices rose sharply in some months and eased in others, and those changes moved the overall inflation rate up and down. The underlying rate moved within a much narrower range and never fell far. Inflation in 2026 did not rise steadily, and it never cooled enough to give households relief. It stayed high.

According to recent reports, CNBC tracked how U.S. consumer price inflation changed across each month of 2026. Over those months, underlying inflation cooled during the summer, and prices rose again in the autumn as energy and transport costs climbed. The October figures are the most recent. The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2.0%, and underlying inflation did not come close to that goal in any of those months. Read one month at a time, the year looks less like a steady climb than a series of ups and downs that never brought prices near the Fed's target. The question for the months ahead is whether the autumn rise is a fresh problem or the same one returning.

January looked calm only because a month of strong income covered a problem that was already built into prices.

February's rise ran through the whole budget, with no single shock for families to wait out.

In March, the part of inflation that leaves out food and energy stayed high and showed no sign of easing. Core prices were 3.2% higher than a year earlier, according to CNBC, and the BEA reports that they rose 0.3% from February alone. March brought a sudden jump in overall prices, but the more lasting problem was that the base underneath that jump kept going up every month. Whatever happened to groceries and fuel that spring, households already faced an underlying rate above 3%.

Sources indicate that the jump that made March stand out came from food and energy, not from a broad newly introduced wave of price increases. Overall prices were 0.7% higher than in February, according to the BEA, far faster than the core measure. Core leaves out only food and energy, so those two categories account for the difference. That was the spring pattern of a stuck year, with sharp increases in the cost of essentials on top of a base that kept rising at a steadier pace. A narrow increase was still no comfort to a household, because it hit the purchases people can't put off.

In a recent development, when groceries and fuel cost more, the same paycheck buys less right away. That drop is small on its own. But it came while the underlying rate stayed above 3%, and that combination is how a stuck year costs families: not through a single shock, but through a steady loss of buying power that one bad month makes larger.

March's jump came from essentials, but the base beneath it kept climbing.

With the income dip set aside, April left a level of price pressure that set the bar for the rest of the year.

Households in May faced a broader rise in prices than the underlying rate alone would suggest. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, were 3.4% higher than a year earlier, according to CNBC, while the BEA reports that the full basket of consumer prices was up 4.1%. Core leaves out only food and energy, so the higher overall figure means those two categories had become more expensive than the rest of the budget over the previous 12 months. For a family, the higher number is the one that counts, because groceries and gas are purchases no one can skip.

According to recent reports, shoppers spent more freely in May, but much of the extra money only covered higher prices. The BEA reports that consumer spending rose 0.7% in dollars during the month and only 0.3% once price changes are taken out. The busy checkout lines of May reflected inflation as much as demand. Households paid noticeably more and came home with only modestly more.

Personal income rose 0.7% in dollars, matching the rise in spending, according to the BEA, and farm income in the month was tied to payments under the American Relief Act of 2025. May's income figure combines ordinary earnings with government aid to a single industry. Only the earnings show how most households were doing as prices kept rising.

In May, households paid more for essentials while the core rate kept creeping up.

The relief households got in June depended on the most volatile prices they pay, and those prices can rise again as rapidly as they fell.

Recent findings suggest that whether underlying inflation cooled in July depends on which count of the month a reader trusts. By the later count, core prices, which leave out food and energy, were 3.0% higher than a year earlier, according to CNBC, down from 3.3% in June. In its first estimate for the month, BEA puts the annual core rate at 3.3%, the same as June's. By that first count, underlying inflation held still from June to July rather than easing. One count shows a real summer dip, and the other shows no change at all.

The gap between the two counts does not have to mean that one of them is wrong. The 3.3% reading was the first estimate for July, and BEA reports that an annual enhancement of its figures was still to come after that release. The 3.0% reading comes from a record of the full year compiled months later, so revisions may account for the cooler number. Nothing in the figures shows that they do. That leaves the summer cooling an open question. Anyone who reads 2026 as the year inflation eased in summer is relying on the more favorable of the two counts.

In a recent development, under either count, July gave households a pause rather than relief. Americans bought almost nothing more than they had in June. Spending adjusted for prices rose by only $1.3 billion in July, according to BEA, which is close to no growth at all in an economy the size of the U.S. Households did not buy more even in a month when the underlying rate, by the later count, had cooled. A cooler number on paper and flat buying in stores add up to a pause, not a recovery.

Whatever July's true reading, the problem had not ended when autumn arrived.

What set August apart was that households bought more with the money they spent. Spending adjusted for prices rose 0.5% in the month, according to BEA, which outpaced the month's rise in prices. Americans came home with more goods and services rather than just bigger bills. That is what a real lull looks like for a family, which gets more for its money instead of only paying more for the same things.

August was the last month of 2026 so far in which households got more for their money.

It has been revealed that prices picked up again in September. The overall price index climbed 0.5% from August, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data reported by CNBC. Much of the increase came from energy and transport costs, which Americans pay to fuel their cars and get around. Households can't easily cut back on those costs.

The underlying rate of inflation rose more slowly than the headline rate. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, were up 0.3% in September. It has been revealed that in the news release, PayKings Offers Free Statement Analyzer That Shows High-Risk Merchants the Rate They Actually Pay, issued 25-Nov-2026 by PayKings over PR Newswire, we are advised by the firm that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:.

In a recent development, A merchant quoted 2.6% can pay 3.5% once every fee is counted. The free tool finds the real number in about a minute.

Recent findings suggest that LEHI, Utah, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- PayKings, a high-risk merchant services provider, offers a free Statement Analyzer that shows merchants the actual rate they pay to accept cards. Merchants upload a statement from any U.S. processor and receive their effective rate, total fees, and a line-by-line breakdown in about a minute.

Recent findings suggest that most merchants know the rate printed on their contract, but the effective rate tells a different story. Calculated by dividing total processing fees by total card volume, it includes charges that contract rates may leave out, such as per-transaction, monthly, and PCI fees. A merchant quoted 2.6% can end up paying 3.5%. The analyzer works with any U.S. merchant statement, including those from CBD, firearms, nutraceutical, and telemedicine businesses PayKings specializes in.

"Most merchants we talk to have never seen their real processing rate," said Kyle Hall, CEO of PayKings. "They see one number on a contract and assume that's what they're paying, but the reality is often much more complicated. We believe every business owner deserves complete transparency into their processing fees so they can understand exactly where their money is going and make informed decisions about their business.".

Account and routing numbers are masked in every result. The tool is free, requires no obligation, and can also be used by anyone reviewing a statement shared by a merchant.

The Statement Analyzer is available at https://paykings.com/tools/statement-analyzer/?utm_source=prnewswire&utm_medium=press_release&utm_campaign=statement_analyzer.

Founded in 2011, PayKings has offices in Lehi, Utah, and St. Petersburg, Florida. The tech giant specializes in payment processing for high-risk businesses, with more than 20 acquiring bank relationships and service across 50+ industries, including CBD, firearms, nutraceuticals, and telemedicine. PayKings approves 86% of merchants who apply. Learn more at https://paykings.com/. PayKings, 2901 Bluegrass Blvd, Suite 200-338, Lehi, UT 84043.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

It has been revealed that A newly introduced baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

Sources indicate that “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla stated. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has concerns with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and Latest Jersey.

In a recent development, gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla remarked. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for consumers.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

Industry observers note that birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

In a recent development, the impossible research burden on latest parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

It has been revealed that how universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

It has been revealed that that “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our company has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, walmart is known for its bargains, but its growth increasingly comes from shoppers who don’t strictly need them. Six-figure households like a good deal, too.

Upper-income households led Walmart’s U.S. market-share gains, the organization said Nov. 19 as it reported fiscal third-quarter results. Revenue rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion from $179.5 billion a year earlier and topped Wall Street’s forecasts for both sales and profit.

E-commerce did the heavy lifting. U.S. online sales rose 23%, the 11th straight quarter up more than 20%, while global e-commerce grew 17%.

In a recent development, “We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” CEO John Furner stated in the release. Walmart raised its full-year outlook for the third time this year and now expects net sales growth of 4.9% to 5.2% and adjusted earnings per share of $2.84 to $2.89, up from $2.80 to $2.87.

It has been revealed that not everything accelerated. U.S. comparable sales rose 2.9%, well below the 4.5% gain a year earlier, and the new outlook came in more conservative than analysts expected, the Associated Press reported.

The split matters well beyond Bentonville. With more than 150 million customers shopping its stores or website each week, Walmart is one of the clearest windows into American spending heading into the holidays, and right now that window highlights higher earners stepping up while others pull back.

Furner mentioned in February that most of Walmart’s share gains came from households earning more than $100,000, and in June he told reporters that higher-income customers were visiting more often and buying more.

The newly introduced customers also skew young. At Sam’s Club, Gen Z and millennials made up more than half of new sign-ups in the quarter, and more than half of that group chose the pricier Plus tier.

According to recent reports, convenience is a big part of the pitch. Mobile ordering, free pickup, and fast delivery let customers fill a grocery cart, pick up prescriptions, and stock the garden in one stop, and Walmart remarked its biggest market-share gains in three years came in food, CNBC reported.

Industry observers note that membership is the next lever. In October, Walmart rolled out a $120-a-year bundle of Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus, nearly $100 less than buying both separately.

“It does help at a time when we do see some customers showing some signs of pressure,” Furner told Fox News Digital at the launch, pointing to higher energy costs.

It has been revealed that walmart’s stores power its online business. The company said more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders, including third-party marketplace orders, are fulfilled from stores, letting it deliver a wide assortment faster.

Industry observers note that fuel costs have tested that network this year. Diesel hit a record national average of $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, according to AAA, a surge CBS News reported was especially painful for farmers and small businesses.

Sources indicate that prices have since eased, with diesel falling below $6 in mid-November for the first time in two months as President Trump signaled he wouldn’t escalate the war in Iran. Furner told CNBC the retailer aims to keep prices low despite fuel costs, and Walmart ended the quarter with about 7,700 rollbacks.

Advertising is padding the margins. Walmart U.S. ad sales rose 37% in the quarter, and WARC platform benchmarks put Walmart’s average return on ad spend about 25% above Amazon’s.

Industry observers note that walmart’s global ad business brought in roughly $6.4 billion last fiscal year, per WARC. That’s far behind Amazon’s roughly $68 billion but well ahead of Target’s Roundel and of Instacart and DoorDash combined.

Not every customer is on board. Numerator data released days before the earnings report demonstrated Walmart stores lost 5.6% of their low-income purchasing households, and the ones who stayed made fewer trips.

Among low-income shoppers cutting back on Walmart store visits, 51% named Amazon as an alternative, ahead of local grocery stores and dollar stores.

Industry observers note that that rivalry has already cost Walmart a crown. Amazon ended Walmart’s 13-year run atop the Fortune 500 this year, and Walmart now ranks No. 2 on the 2026 Fortune 500, with $713.2 billion in revenue.

Furner’s answer is to pull every part of the business into the fight. “From membership and agentic shopping to upcoming ways of using our stores and delivery network, we’re bringing the best of Walmart together to serve customers better and create new opportunities for growth,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, karpelès’ warning comes as Pump.fun has set a Nov.
  • But to maintain their current accounts, Pump.fun is asking users to import their private keys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès has strongly warned owners of Solana-based memecoin launchpad Pump.fun about potential major security risks associated with the new wallet migration process, which could put users' private keys at great risk.

According to recent reports, karpelès’ warning comes as Pump.fun has set a Nov. 30 deadline to stop allowing external wallet logins to its website. The platform is moving to email and social logins, which will enable people to access their accounts via Google, Apple and GitHub.

But to maintain their current accounts, Pump.fun is asking users to import their private keys. This is what Karpelès thinks could compromise the security of their crypto assets.

In a recent X post, Karpelès noted he studied Pump.fun's JavaScript code to understand the nature of the new migration process.

The analysis has raised questions about the security of people’ private keys, despite the platform's claims.

“At best, it's a misnomer to refer to it as 'end-to-end encryption,'” noted Karpelès.

According to Karpelès, owners' private keys are first encrypted in their browsers before being sent through Pump.fun’s servers to the platform’s wallet infrastructure provider, Privy.

Industry observers note that also, Pump.fun's backend provides the public key used for encryption during migration. People’ browsers have no way to check whether the public key is authentic, according to Karpelès.

The possibility of a security breach involving Privy’s infrastructure is another major concern.

“Your money also now relies on Privy never getting hacked,” Karpelès warned.

One of the most important aspects of Karpelès' warning is the need for migration in the first place.

He said Pump.fun could use signature-based authentication without forcing users to expose their private keys.

Pump.fun already uses a "Sign in with Solana" message to prove ownership of a wallet, according to Karpelès.

So theoretically, people can prove ownership of their wallets and execute transactions without having to import their private credentials into a new system.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.
  • It has been revealed that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT.
  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

It has been revealed that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Recent findings suggest that blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

In a recent development, if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

Sources indicate that the FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It demonstrates how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Sources indicate that binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:.

It has been revealed that the first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what consumers hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Recent findings suggest that why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

Recent findings suggest that how Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

Sources indicate that what the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It demonstrates the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance claims the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest revision says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

It has been revealed that what customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

3 forces moving SPCX stock on Tesla merger talk that has no terms

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dilution fears, merger arbitrage and S&P 500 hopes all move SPCX stock, yet each rests on Tesla deal terms that no one has set.
  • Investors are trading SpaceX shares around a possible merger with Tesla $TSLA whose price and structure nobody has set.
  • According to recent reports, the people closest to the deal speak warmly about the idea but have not committed to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dilution fears, merger arbitrage and S&P 500 hopes all move SPCX stock, yet each rests on Tesla deal terms that no one has set.

Investors are trading SpaceX shares around a possible merger with Tesla $TSLA whose price and structure nobody has set. SpaceX's amended IPO filing warned that the firm may sell a large amount of upcoming stock to pay for future deals, according to CNBC, and investors have read that warning with Tesla in mind. Every trade in SPCX that turns on the merger is a bet on terms that do not yet exist.

According to recent reports, the people closest to the deal speak warmly about the idea but have not committed to it. "There's no question that there are synergies between Tesla and SpaceX in our futures," Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and COO, told CNBC. Both companies have set up board committees to weigh a deal, yet no transaction has won the backing of either board. Elon Musk also cannot push a deal through on his own. CNBC reports that Musk has acknowledged shareholders would need to approve a merger first, and he is barred from taking part directly in the negotiations of those committees. Until that process produces terms, every number attached to a Tesla-SpaceX merger is an assumption, and investors should weigh each claim about SPCX with that in mind.

In a recent development, yahoo Finance has laid out why SPCX shares have been moving amid the Tesla merger talks, from traders betting against the stock to the hope that a deal could open the door to the S&P 500. Shareholders have already paid for the uncertainty. SpaceX priced its IPO at $135 per share, according to CNBC. SPCX traded as low as $119.51 on Nov. 25 after a one-day drop of 5.01%, so anyone who got shares at the IPO price is now holding a loss. Most of the arguments for buying or selling the stock depend on the shape of a deal, meaning a price and a share swap that no one has set. Each argument is only as solid as the assumption beneath it. Some of the pressure on SPCX would remain even if no merger happened. Investors who separate the two kinds of pressure can tell which worries would likely fade once terms emerge and which would stay.

It has been revealed that what worries SPCX holders most is not a merger itself but the number of new shares SpaceX might have to issue if it paid for Tesla $TSLA in stock. Yahoo Finance ranks that fear first among the forces weighing on the stock. Gary Black, managing partner of The Future Fund, estimated in a post on X $TWTR that a Tesla deal could mean roughly 52% more SpaceX shares. A possible acquisition of Cursor, by contrast, would dilute existing holders by 3.4% measured at the IPO valuation, according to CNBC. For anyone who holds SPCX, a Tesla deal on the scale Black describes would leave each existing share representing a much smaller part of the company.

The 52% figure describes one possible scenario, and its size depends on the inputs Black chose. His estimate assumes SpaceX pays a 25% premium for Tesla. A smaller premium would require fewer latest shares, and a larger one would require more. The estimate also assumes an all-stock deal, so if SpaceX paid any part of the price in another form, it would issue fewer shares. Investors are right that a stock deal would dilute their holdings, but the size of that dilution depends on two assumptions that no one has confirmed.

According to recent reports, the public holders who would share the dilution have little say in the company. Musk controls 82.4% of SpaceX's voting power after the IPO, according to CNBC, which leaves outside shareholders with a small share of the votes. SPCX buyers can factor the dilution risk into the price they pay, but their votes carry little weight against his.

SPCX holders should treat dilution as a cost they may have to accept rather than a decision they control.

Industry observers note that part of the selling in SPCX comes from SpaceX's role in the hypothetical deal, not from any judgment about its rocket business. In the merger investors are imagining, SpaceX would be the acquirer. Traders who bet on mergers buy the organization being acquired and short the buyer, so SPCX lands on the side being sold whatever SpaceX's own prospects look like. Those traders keep selling SPCX until terms emerge, and no one has offered any. The selling rests on a deal structure that doesn't exist yet, and it says nothing about how SpaceX runs its business.

The traders are betting on a gap that no one can measure. The two companies haven't agreed how Tesla $TSLA stock would convert into SpaceX stock, so traders have no locked-in profit to aim for, only a guess at what the terms might turn out to be. Regulatory scrutiny could also block a SpaceX-Tesla merger, according to CNBC. Closing is expected to take at least 12 months, Yahoo Finance reports, so arbitrage traders would carry the risk of a blocked deal for at least a year even after terms appear. SPCX holders shouldn't expect the selling to end neatly once terms are announced.

Arbitrage can't explain every drop in SPCX. SpaceX shares were down about 9% one Thursday afternoon, and Tesla shares about 11%, during a broad sell-off in tech stocks, according to CNBC. Tesla fell even though arbitrage traders are buyers of its stock, and the sell-off reached well beyond the two companies, so SPCX holders lost value that day for reasons that went beyond the merger trade.

The political backdrop adds pressure that a deal wouldn't remove. "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop," Deutsche Bank analysts noted in a note, as reported by CNBC. That kind of weakness would remain whether or not SpaceX and Tesla ever combine.

Only the arbitrage part of SPCX's slide depends on the merger's terms, and the rest is likely to stay after those terms arrive.

In a recent development, SPCX holders have one argument for buying rather than selling. A merger with Tesla $TSLA, already a member of the S&P 500, could put SpaceX on a fast track into the index and potentially set off buying by index funds, according to JPMorgan $JPM analysts, as reported by Yahoo Finance. The analysts describe a possible effect of a deal that no one has agreed to, so the upside can be no more real than the merger itself. Investors who expect a shortcut point to SpaceX's size, but the firm that runs the index has already turned down that argument. S&P Global $SPGI said, as reported by CNBC, that "exceptions to the financial viability, seasoning, and IWF (investable weight factor) requirements should not be granted solely based on market capitalization.".

In a recent development, spaceX can't qualify on its own because it loses money. The company lost $4.94 billion in 2025, according to CNBC, and Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth, praises S&P for insisting that companies earn a profit before they join. That loss is why investors treat the merger as a back door. A deal could also let SpaceX skip the 12-month wait that a newly listed stock normally serves before it can join. S&P has not stated how it would treat SpaceX as part of a company already in the index, so holders are betting on a ruling no one has made. A possible index lift that depends on an unapproved deal and an open rules question is a weak reason to buy SPCX today.

Index funds will have reasons to buy SpaceX that don't involve Tesla. The Nasdaq $NDAQ 100 has already changed its rules to ease entry for the largest companies, CNBC reports, and S&P intends to modify entry rules for the S&P Total Market Index and the Dow Jones U.S. Total Stock Market Index to give SpaceX a path in. S&P is holding its line only at the flagship S&P 500.

The index buying that is coming doesn't depend on Tesla, and the part that does is the least certain piece of the story.

  • Industry observers note that microsoft intends to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Industry observers note that microsoft intends to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft claims Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft unveiled Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and mentioned it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Recent findings suggest that reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist consumers may end up back with the people who built it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WASHINGTON, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) today welcomed an order by the United States District Court for the District of Maryland granting summary judgment in favor of the Commission and dismissing Amazon.com, Inc.'s challenge to the Commission's orders concerning more than 400,000 hazardous consumer products.

Central to this litigation was the question of Amazon's status as a regulated entity under the Consumer Product Safety Act in connection with its Fulfilment by Amazon program. Through its administrative proceedings and subsequent defense of its orders in federal court, the Commission has sought to establish legal clarity regarding Amazon's obligations under federal product safety law. The court's decision marks an vital milestone in clarifying the application of the Act to modern e-commerce business models.

Recent findings suggest that in July 2024, the Commission unanimously determined that Amazon acted as a distributor under the Consumer Product Safety Act when it distributed certain hazardous products through its Fulfilment by Amazon program and therefore bore legal responsibility for their recall. The products included faulty carbon monoxide detectors, hair dryers lacking required electrocution protection, and children's sleepwear that failed to comply with federal flammability standards.

Sources indicate that "This is an important victory for American consumers and a significant step toward greater regulatory certainty in the e-commerce marketplace," said CPSC Acting Chairman Peter A. Feldman. "American families deserve the same consumer safety protections under federal law whether they shop online or in a brick-and-mortar store.".

The court's November 24, 2026, order denied Amazon's motion for summary judgment, granted the defendants' cross-motion for summary judgment, entered judgment in favor of the defendants, and dismissed Amazon's complaint challenging the Commission's January 2025 Decision and Order.

In a recent development, CPSC appreciates the work of its attorneys and career staff who have contributed to this matter over the past five years, as well as the attorneys at the U.S. Department of Justice who successfully defended the Commission's action in federal court.

SOURCE U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.

XRP's sharp price decline might have finally stopped, as the asset has started to form a trading range that could provide a foundation for a recovery going forward. The most likely support level here is $0.9, as the price has already tested it three times.

According to recent reports, the rapid downfall of XRP began on November 5, essentially marking the beginning of a sharp decline for the asset. The failure to break above the 100 EMA effectively eliminated the possibility of an uptrend. The price failed to break the mid-term trend and declined rapidly.
