📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A wave of Democrat support in the midterms swept across the U.S. in the beginning of November marking a change of power in politics—not just from the flipping of red to blue, but also from old to young: non-boomer politicians in Congress are at their highest point since the turn of the century. But even as the Baby Boomers are losing their hold on political power, their economic influence remains considerably more difficult to dislodge.

Industry observers note that americans born between 1946 and 1964 still control more than half of the nation’s wealth, despite representing a continuously shrinking share of the population. And their financial advantage has implications for younger generations struggling with housing costs, student debt and the rising cost of living—especially as the transfer of wealth from older generations to their children remains sluggish.

In a recent development, the shift away from Baby Boomer leadership in government has been building for years, but the 2026 midterms accelerated the transition. For the first time in decades, the generation that dominated congressional leadership and policymaking is losing its grip.

According to recent reports, the House already moved past the point of Boomer dominance. According to Pew Research Center, Boomers accounted for 39% of House members at the beginning of the 119th Congress, down from a majority just two Congresses earlier. Gen X became the largest generation in the chamber, representing 41% of lawmakers while Millennials accounted for another 15%. The Senate has been slower to change. Boomers still represent 60 of 99 senators at the beginning of the 119th Congress, or roughly 61%.

Sources indicate that but that imbalance is beginning to change. According to Quorum’s analysis of newly elected lawmakers, Gen X and Millennials account for 87% of the incoming 120th Congressional class. Of the 120 new members, just 13 are Boomers—while 56 Gen Xers and 48 Millennials will occupy the new seats.

Sources indicate that the change is also visible in the pipeline of candidates seeking office. Future Caucus found that Millennials and Gen Z accounted for roughly one-third of congressional candidates in 2026, up from one-quarter in 2024 and one-sixth in 2022. According to the report, Millennials also became the largest generational group running for Senate for the first time in the report’s history.

Sources indicate that still, the political transition is not complete as the Senate continues to be a stubborn stronghold for older Americans. The incoming chamber’s median age will fall to 63 from 64, but will still remain among the oldest Senates in American history, according to Reuters.

According to the Federal Reserve’s Distributional Financial Accounts, Baby Boomers held approximately $97.4 trillion in household net worth in Q2 2026. That represents 52.5% of all U.S. household wealth, despite Boomers accounting for just 27% of the country’s adult population.

Industry observers note that in contrast, Millennials and Gen Z together represented 22.4% of real estate but only held 11.2% of household wealth—about $20.8 trillion. Generation X held another 25.7%.

In a recent development, and while the great wealth transfer is coming, younger Americans are waiting. Visa’s Business and Economic Insights report in July estimated approximately $36 trillion of Baby Boomers’ $93 trillion in assets could transfer to younger generations over the next 20 years—after accounting for liabilities, taxes, fees, retirement spending and other exclusions.

It has been revealed that “Imagine you are sitting on a winning lottery ticket. You hit the jackpot, but you immediately lose half by— smartly—taking the lump sum,” the report read. “Next, you lose another 30–40 percent through taxes and fees. The advertised jackpot is enormous, but after the lump-sum haircut, taxes and fees, the take-home number is much lower. A similar dynamic applies to the great wealth transfer.”.

According to recent reports, but that doesn’t mean the younger Americans will now get access to that same financial security. The transfer is likely to be uneven, with most of the wealth being concentrated among families that already have substantial assets.

According to Visa’s research, nearly 75% of inheritance recipients already have higher net worths than the average household. That means much of the inherited wealth from the transfer will be saved or invested, not immediately spent. Visa also estimated that one in four millennial homeowners received financial assistance from their parents for a down payment.

But perspective matters. A 2025 analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis found that Millennials and Gen Z households actually had more inflation-adjusted wealth at approximately age 34 than Boomers did at that same age.

According to the analysis, Millennials and Gen Zers owned $1.23 for every $1 of wealth owned by Gen Xers at the same age—and $1.35 for every $1 of wealth owned by baby boomers.

The generational war has a six-year deadline, set by Social Security and the national debt.

According to the 2026 Social Security trustees report, the combined retirement and disability trust funds are projected to be depleted by 2032. At that point, incoming revenue would only cover 83% of scheduled benefits unless Congress changes the program.

Sources indicate that boomers have held the presidency since 2001, spanning George W. Bush to Donald Trump, with the exception of Joe Biden—who is part of the Silent Generation. In that time span, the national debt climbed from $5.81 trillion to over $40.17 trillion through September 2026, according to the Treasury’s fiscal data, during which time, they have passed a series of tax cuts leaving their own generation’s retirements endangered.

Democrats have argued for increasing revenue by raising the cap on earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes, while Republicans mostly emphasized economic growth. But Sen. Ron Johnson—the Wisconsin Republican who chairs the Senate Budget Committee and is a Boomer himself—has a typically Boomerian fix: make other generations pay for it.

It has been revealed that social Security is funded primarily through payroll taxes paid by today’s workers, meaning younger Americans now are financing the benefits for current retirees. But once the funds are depleted, covering the shortfall would mean borrowing more from other federal priorities. In effect, the government would be putting the cost of maintaining the retirement benefits on the national credit card, leaving younger taxpayers to help service the debt through future taxes or spending cuts.

In a recent development, on Nov. 18, Johnson called Social Security a “legal Ponzi scheme” on Fox Business. The following day, he remarked Congress should first pass legislation preventing benefit cuts and then address what he described as the country’s massive debt. He also introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act, allowing the Treasury’s general fund to cover Social Security benefits after it becomes insolvent. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates the approach would add $190 trillion to the federal debt over 75 years.

NFL guarantees explained, from skill and injury protection to dead money

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Guaranteed money in NFL contracts comes in several forms, from signing bonuses to vesting guarantees, and this guide explains how each works and when teams can void it.
  • It has been revealed that A signing bonus is guaranteed money that an NFL player is owed for agreeing to a contract.
  • It has been revealed that that even split is called proration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Guaranteed money in NFL contracts comes in several forms, from signing bonuses to vesting guarantees, and this guide explains how each works and when teams can void it.

It has been revealed that A signing bonus is guaranteed money that an NFL player is owed for agreeing to a contract. For salary-cap purposes, the league does not count it all at once. The bonus is spread evenly over the years of the deal, up to a maximum of five years.

It has been revealed that that even split is called proration. Each season covered by the deal carries an equal share of the bonus on the team's books. The share does not change based on how the player performs or how many games he plays. Because the shares are fixed at signing, a team knows the bonus charge for every season of the deal in advance.

The five-year ceiling shapes how longer contracts are counted. On a three-year deal, the bonus is divided into three equal parts. On a five-year deal, it is divided into five. On a deal that runs longer than five years, the bonus is still split over just five seasons. The seasons beyond that carry none of it.

A fully guaranteed contract protects a player's money against every standard reason a team might stop paying. Those reasons are release for performance, an injury suffered on the job and a cut made for salary-cap purposes.

Industry observers note that when that protection is in place at signing, the team is committed to the full amount from the first day. No later date or condition has to pass before the money is secure.

In a recent development, most NFL deals work differently. A typical contract guarantees only part of its value. The team can release the player and owe nothing beyond that part. Some contracts also carry one type of guarantee without the others. A player might be covered if he is hurt on the job but not if he is cut for performance.

A fully guaranteed contract closes those gaps. Releasing the player does not erase what he is owed. Poor play, an injury or a tight salary cap does not change the total either.

Dead money is the salary cap charge a team still carries for a player who is no longer on its roster. It is made up of guaranteed money and unamortized bonus money that remain on the cap after a release or trade.

Bonus money turns into dead money because of a gap between when it is paid and when it is counted. The player collects the bonus, but the team books its cap charge in yearly installments. If he leaves before every installment has been counted, the remaining ones do not vanish. They still have to land on the cap.

Sources indicate that guaranteed salary follows the same logic. If a contract protects a player's pay for a future season and the team cuts him, the club still owes that money. The amount counts against the cap even though the player will never take another snap for the team.

According to recent reports, void years are placeholder seasons added to the end of an NFL contract for one reason: to stretch how a bonus is counted against the salary cap. The player is not expected to play them.

In a recent development, the tool builds on signing bonus accounting. A bonus is charged to the cap in equal shares across a contract's years, with proration capped at five years.

Void years work inside that rule. Each added season counts as a contract year for proration purposes. More years on paper means the bonus is divided into more shares. Each share is smaller. The bonus charge in every season the player actually plays shrinks as a result.

That is the point of the structure. A team carries a lower cap figure while the player is on its roster. The rest of the cost is pushed into seasons when he will not be there.

According to recent reports, an NFL team can generally seek to void guarantees or recover bonus money when a player breaches his contract. Failing to report, retiring and being suspended are among the breaches that can open that door.

In a recent development, A guarantee is a promise from the team, but it rests on the player meeting his own obligations under the deal. When a player stops meeting them, the team can argue that its side of the promise no longer holds.

It has been revealed that that is why a guarantee is not unconditional. Its protections cover a release for performance, injury or salary-cap reasons. A breach by the player is a separate matter.

Failing to report is one example. A player who holds out from training camp or skips mandatory team activities is not providing the services his contract calls for. That absence can give the team grounds to challenge money it agreed to guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that an NFL contract has two numbers that matter. One is the total value revealed on signing day. The other is the portion a player is certain to collect. Those figures are often far apart. The gap between them shapes how teams build rosters, manage the salary cap and decide when to move on from a player.

Industry observers note that most NFL contracts are not guaranteed in full. A team can release a player and owe him nothing beyond the guaranteed portion of his deal. That makes guaranteed money in NFL contracts the clearer measure of what a deal is worth to the player. It is also the clearer measure of how much risk a team has taken on.

In a recent development, guarantees are not a single category. Some money is protected only if a player is injured on the job. Some is protected against a release for performance reasons or for salary-cap reasons. Some is protected against all of those at once. That is what "fully guaranteed" means. Money can also change status over time. It can start with limited protection and become fully guaranteed on a set date.

Recent findings suggest that the signing bonus sits at the center of many deals. It is guaranteed to the player. The team, however, spreads its cap charge evenly across the contract, up to a maximum of five years. That accounting choice shapes much of what happens later. It feeds into dead money, the cap charges that remain after a player is released or traded. It also explains why teams use the post-June 1 designation. And it explains why some contracts include void years that a player is not expected to play.

Industry observers note that guarantees also have limits. Offset language can reduce what a former team owes once a released player signs elsewhere. A team can also try to void guarantees or recover bonus money when a player breaches his contract. Failing to report, retiring and being suspended are examples. Whether that effort succeeds depends on the contract's language and the collective bargaining agreement between the league and the players' union. Sometimes it depends on an arbitrator.

According to recent reports, most of the money in an NFL contract is not guaranteed. A team can release a player and owe him nothing beyond the guaranteed portion of his deal, however many years or dollars remain on paper.

That makes the declared value a best-case figure rather than a promise. A deal is usually reported with a length and a total. That total assumes the player stays on the roster for every season of the contract.

If the team cuts him early, the unguaranteed salary in the remaining years is never paid. The player keeps only what the team committed to in advance. Everything above that amount depends on the club's ongoing decision to keep employing him.

It has been revealed that the guaranteed figure is the part of the deal a player can count on. It is owed whether or not he finishes the contract. The unguaranteed remainder works more like a series of future choices the team can make or decline.

Guaranteed money can take more than one form. A signing bonus is guaranteed to the player. Salary for a given season can also be guaranteed, either fully or only against specific risks such as injury.

This explains why two contracts with similar totals can mean very different things for the people who sign them. One deal may protect a large share of its value. Another may protect only a small slice, leaving most of the reported total tied to future roster decisions.

The split matters to teams as well. Unguaranteed money disappears when a player is released. The guaranteed portion is the commitment a club cannot walk away from. Releasing a player saves a team only the unguaranteed part of his remaining pay.

In a recent development, the guaranteed amount, not the total, demonstrates how secure a player's pay is. How much is guaranteed, in what form and from which date are the details that decide what a player collects.

Sources indicate that proration is an accounting rule, not a payment schedule. It governs how the bonus counts against the cap. It does not determine when the money reaches the player. The timing of the actual payments is a separate matter set by the contract.

Recent findings suggest that that separation lets a team commit a large sum to a player while counting only a fraction of it against the cap in any single season. The bonus can keep appearing on the cap sheet in seasons after the cash has already been paid.

Industry observers note that for the player, the value lies in the guarantee. A signing bonus belongs to the protected part of a deal, not the part a team can walk away from by releasing him.

Recent findings suggest that that sets it apart from much of a contract's headline value. Salary scheduled for later seasons may never be paid if the player is released first. A release does not cancel the signing bonus.

Industry observers note that the size of the bonus also affects how much of a deal is protected. A contract built around a large signing bonus and modest yearly salaries puts more of its value into guaranteed money. A deal with a small bonus leaves more of its value exposed to an early release.

NFL guarantees come in three main types, and each covers a different reason a team might cut a player. A skill guarantee protects against release for performance, an injury guarantee protects a player hurt on the job, and a cap guarantee protects a player released for salary-cap reasons.

The skill guarantee covers a judgment about ability. If a club releases a player because it decides he is no longer good enough, a skill guarantee means it still owes the protected amount. The decision to move on does not cancel the obligation.

The injury guarantee is tied to a specific event. It applies when a player is hurt while performing his job for the team. If that injury leads to his release, the guaranteed salary remains payable. It does not shield him from a release driven by declining play or by budget pressure.

The cap guarantee covers a third scenario. Teams operate under a salary cap, and a club sometimes cuts a player to clear room for other spending. A cap guarantee means that reason alone does not let the team walk away from the protected money.

Sources indicate that these categories are separate promises. A contract can include any combination of the three. Some deals protect money against only one risk, while others stack two or all three on the same salary.

A single guaranteed total does not show which protection applies to each dollar. Money shielded only against injury gives a healthy player little security if his performance slips. Money with only a cap guarantee does not help him if the team cuts him for poor play.

It has been revealed that each protection is defined by the reason for ending the deal. That makes the reason for a release central to what the player collects. Two players cut on the same day for the same reason can leave with very different sums, depending on which protections their contracts carry.

Reading guarantee language comes down to two questions: how much money is protected, and against which of the three risks.

Kirk Cousins signed one of these deals with the Minnesota Vikings in 2018. It was a three-year contract worth $84 million, and the entire amount was fully guaranteed.

In a recent development, deshaun Watson's 2022 contract with the Cleveland Browns followed the same structure on a larger scale. It covered five years and $230 million, all of it fully guaranteed.

It has been revealed that full guarantees also appear at the start of some careers. First-round rookie contracts are typically fully guaranteed. A team that drafts a player in the first round is usually committed to his whole rookie deal from the day he signs it.

Industry observers note that players drafted in later rounds face a different arrangement. Their contracts more often guarantee only the signing bonus. The rest of their salary is not protected. A team can release them and owe nothing beyond that bonus.

The split between those two groups ties financial security to draft position. A first-round pick usually holds a fully guaranteed deal from signing. A later-round pick often keeps each season's salary only by staying on the roster.

Industry observers note that A vesting date is the point at which a limited guarantee becomes a full one. Some contract guarantees protect a salary against injury only at first, then become fully guaranteed on a set date, usually tied to the start of the league year.

It has been revealed that before that date, the protection is narrow. An injury-only guarantee covers a player who gets hurt on the job. It does not cover a release for performance or for salary-cap reasons. A healthy player cut ahead of the vesting date can leave without that money.

After the date passes, the same salary is protected against all three of those risks. The team owes it whether the player is cut for skill, for injury or to clear cap space. The dollar amount does not change on the vesting date. What changes is the set of circumstances in which the team must pay it.

In a recent development, that structure turns the vesting date into a decision point. A team that wants to move on from a player has a reason to act before the guarantee locks in. A team that keeps the player past that date has, in effect, committed to the salary. For the player, the date marks when an expected payment becomes one he can count on.

Recent findings suggest that the fifth-year option on a first-round pick follows this pattern. When a team exercises the option, the salary for that extra season is guaranteed for injury only. It becomes fully guaranteed on the first day of the league year. Until then, the team keeps some flexibility over a player it has already chosen to retain.

Sources indicate that the franchise tag works differently. There is no waiting period tied to the calendar. Franchise-tag salary becomes fully guaranteed once the player signs the tender. The trigger is the player's signature, not a date on the league schedule.

Vesting language also explains why a guaranteed total announced at signing can overstate what is secure on day one. That figure may include money protected only against injury. Checking when each portion vests highlights how much is secure immediately and how much becomes secure later.

In a recent development, non-guaranteed salary works differently. A released player's unprotected base salary comes off the books entirely, and it never becomes dead money. Only protected or already-paid money can leave a charge behind.

A trade can leave dead money behind as well. The original team has already paid the signing bonus. The share of that bonus not yet counted stays on its cap after the player moves to his new club.

This math shapes roster decisions. A release frees only the difference between what the player would have counted and the dead money he leaves behind. When the dead charge is large, a cut can save little cap room that season. In some cases it uses more cap space than keeping the player would have.

Dead money cannot be shifted to another team or wiped off the books. It occupies cap space the team cannot spend on anyone else. A club carrying heavy dead charges has less room to sign free agents or extend its own players.

Recent findings suggest that timing matters too. A separate tool, the post-June 1 designation, changes how the charge is divided across seasons.

An NFL team can designate up to two player releases as post-June 1 cuts. That label spreads the dead money from each of those releases across two seasons instead of loading it into one.

Dead money is the cap charge a team still carries after a player leaves through a release or trade. It can include guaranteed salary the team still owes and bonus money it has not yet counted against the cap. The player is off the roster, but the charge remains.

According to recent reports, the designation changes timing, not size. A released player is still owed every guaranteed dollar his contract promises. The label does not cut his pay, cancel a bonus or reduce what the team must pay him. It moves part of the cap accounting from one season into the next.

The salary cap limits what a team can spend on player pay in a season. A large dead-money charge in one year uses cap space that could otherwise go to other players. Splitting the charge across two seasons lowers the burden in the first one.

The cost is deferred, not avoided. Whatever leaves the first season lands in the second. A team that uses the designation accepts a smaller dead-money charge now in exchange for an added charge the following year.

Bonus proration explains why the split can be large. A signing bonus is guaranteed money for the player, but its cap cost is counted in pieces over the life of the deal. A player released early in a long contract can leave several seasons of uncounted bonus behind. The designation lets a team divide that leftover amount between two seasons rather than absorbing it at once.

The limit of two designations forces a choice. A team weighing several releases must decide which ones gain the most from the split. Releases that leave behind the largest dead-money charges free the most room in the first season.

Sources indicate that the five-year ceiling still limits the math. Void years can stretch proration only as far as that ceiling allows. A deal that already runs five real seasons gains no extra bonus spreading from added years.

It has been revealed that the deferred charge comes due when the contract voids. At that point, the bonus shares assigned to the placeholder seasons have not yet counted. They accelerate onto the cap together rather than spreading over the years they were assigned to.

In a recent development, the same acceleration applies if the team releases or trades the player before the contract reaches its void date. Any bonus shares not yet counted, including those tied to void years, stay on the cap as dead money.

Void years do not change what the player is owed. The signing bonus is guaranteed money either way. The added seasons alter only when its cap charge is recorded, not whether the player collects it.

A void year also differs from an ordinary final season, which a player is under contract to play. It exists on paper for cap accounting, not for games.

Sources indicate that offset language lets a team that releases a player subtract whatever he earns from a latest team from the guaranteed money it still owes him. The clause turns the old team's obligation into a backstop rather than a separate paycheck.

It has been revealed that the clause only matters after a release. Offset language applies to the guaranteed money a team still owes at that point. It does not create a guarantee, and it does not erase one. It changes how much of the remaining guarantee the former team ends up paying.

Industry observers note that the mechanism is subtraction. The former team starts with the guaranteed amount left on the contract. It then deducts what the player earns from his new club. The former team pays whatever is left over.

The effect depends on the size of the newly introduced contract. A player who signs a small deal elsewhere reduces the old team's bill only slightly. A player whose new earnings match or exceed the remaining guarantee can reduce that bill to nothing. In the first case, his combined pay from the two clubs equals the guarantee he was already owed. In the second, it equals his new salary.

Without an offset clause, the arithmetic runs the other way. The former team pays the full remaining guarantee regardless of what happens next. The player keeps that money and also collects whatever his latest team pays him. That outcome is commonly called double-dipping.

The presence or absence of an offset therefore changes what a guarantee is worth in practice. Two contracts with identical guaranteed totals can produce different payouts after a release. The deciding factor is whether the former club is allowed to count the player's fresh earnings against what it owes.

In a recent development, offsets also shape the money a released player can expect from his next deal. With an offset in place, the guarantee from his old team already sets a floor on his income. A fresh contract below that floor shifts who pays him, not how much he receives.

Retirement is a different kind of breach. Here the player chooses to stop playing before his contract runs out. A team in that position can seek to void the guarantees that remain. It can also try to recover signing bonus money it has already paid.

Suspension is a third trigger. A suspended player is unavailable to his team for the games he misses. That absence can give the team grounds to seek to void guarantees.

Recent findings suggest that none of these outcomes is automatic. Whether a team can actually void a guarantee or recoup a bonus turns on three factors. The first is the specific language in the player's contract. The second is the collective bargaining agreement between the NFL and the NFL Players Association. The third, in some disputes, is the ruling of an arbitrator.

Contract language matters because guarantees are negotiated deal by deal. One contract may spell out exactly which conduct cancels a guarantee. Another may be written more narrowly, leaving the team fewer grounds to act.

Recent findings suggest that the collective bargaining agreement sets rules that individual contracts must follow. It shapes what a team may pursue against a player and how disagreements over money are handled.

Sources indicate that when the team and the player read those documents differently, the dispute can go to arbitration. An arbitrator then decides whether a breach occurred. The arbitrator also decides what money, if any, the team can withhold or claim back.

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Sources indicate that testing that more closely replicates the organization’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company indicates it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

Industry observers note that what set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software upgrade that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

Sources indicate that so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July upgrade was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report notes.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Recent findings suggest that third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

According to recent reports, how it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report claims.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft indicates it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also prepares to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

According to recent reports, microsoft states its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it intends to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it states. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

Industry observers note that the upcoming testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the manufacturer notes, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

Elon Musk Backs Binance Founder's Use of Grok AI Assistant

Elon Musk has reacted to a post by Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ), in which the latter shared that he used Grok Bot to tidy up his X following list.

According to CZ, the bot was tasked with removing inactive and abusive accounts from the list of people he follows, though accounts with constructive criticism were supposed to stay. CZ was not fully sure about the results, adding "AI did it" with a shrug emoji.

Musk replied with "Cool." Later, CZ added in the same thread that it "worked well so far.".

According to recent reports, back in September, CZ had to address rumors about his account being hacked after consumers noticed that he had unfollowed a number of profiles. Per CZ, at that time he removed accounts that were inactive for more than 30 days.

Since then, the product has received praise from Nvidia head Jensen Huang, who remarked in October that Grok Bot usage was "really skyrocketing." Musk himself claimed on SpaceX's Q3 earnings call that he had never seen a product grow this fast.

On Coinbase, Grok was responsible for 59.54% of AI-agent trading volume from Sept. 14 to Sept. 21. For comparison, Claude had 13.37% and ChatGPT only 1.54%. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong then named Grok the leading client for agentic traders on the platform, to which Musk also responded with "Cool.".

At the same time, there were complaints. NewCore researchers reported last week that Grok Bot made 31 unrequested access attempts to email, calendar, Slack and GitHub accounts on two employee laptops within five days, ignoring the command to stop.

It was only last month that Musk was trolling Binance after the exchange lost about $6.3 billion in a hack on Oct. 29, the largest one in crypto history so far. Among other things, Musk posted "Everyday is Zeroday" and replied with fire and laughing emojis to CZ's earlier warning about phishing links.

CZ then asked Musk to stop, calling it a "bad time to troll," and reminded him that Binance's $500 million investment in Twitter in 2022 has become a stake in SpaceX worth more than $1 billion.

Now, the two seem to be on good terms again.

Former Pentagon officials say Hegseth blocking senators from visiting Gulf bases amid Iran war ‘smells like a lack of transparency’

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pentagon is banning U.S. lawmakers from visiting Gulf military bases, and former Pentagon officials warn the move is creating tension between the executive and legislative branches and raising questions about why the Department of Defense is limiting access to information about the Iran war.

“It smells like a lack of transparency in order to thwart Congressional oversight, in order to either hide that the Iran war is costing more, or to use the Iran war as an excuse to get more money,” Evelyn Farkas, executive director of the McCain Institute at Arizona State University and former deputy assistant secretary of defense for Russia, Ukraine, and Eurasia, told Fortune.

In a recent development, last month, Connecticut Democrat Sen. Chris Murphy detailed his experience of the Department of Defense barring him from visiting the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar and meeting with military leadership, accusing the Pentagon of obscuring details about the impacts of the Iran war.

It has been revealed that “I have been to the Middle East probably a dozen times at least,” Murphy said in a video uploaded to Facebook. “While I have been a member of Congress, I have never, ever been denied access to military facilities. This is part of a coordinated, deliberate campaign by the Department of Defense to try to hide the consequences and the true cost of this war.”.

Iowa Republican Sen. Joni Ernst was similarly turned away from a base visit around the same time, The Atlantic reported this week. Ernst did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

U.S. Congress members have a long-standing practice of conducting visits of military sites as part of their constitutional oversight. In March, following the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth published a memo to “further discourage visits to the [U.S. Central Command Area of Responsibility] requiring DoW support by members of Congress and their staffs…and no DoW support shall be made available for congressional travel to the USCENTCOM AOR without my approval.”.

Congress has expressed increased misgivings around Hegseth, introducing articles of impeachment this month, which did not pass, in part on the grounds that the secretary began military conflict in Iran without Congressional authorization. Hegseth has sharply reduced the number of routine press briefings and limited press access to briefings, as well as refused to provide information to the Congressional Budget Office ahead of its update to the cost of the Iran war in September. Meanwhile, the Pentagon is seeking $1.5 trillion in allocations—the largest defense budget in U.S. history—to modernize military infrastructure and restock munitions drained in the conflict in the Gulf.

Legislators have been visiting U.S. military bases in times of conflict since at least 1943, when five U.S. senators embarked on a 65-day inspection tour of global military sites during World War II. Visits increased during and after the Vietnam war, when American lawmakers and journalists returned home with stories that vastly differed from former President Richard Nixon’s narrative that the U.S. was winning the war.

Farkas, who served for eight years as a staff member of the Senate Armed Services Committee and took several trips to the Gulf as part of a congressional delegation (CODEL), said congressional visits to these military bases are a way to not only increase public knowledge of the status of a war overseas, but in many cases justify granting the military additional and targeted resources for specific operations.

Recent findings suggest that during the Iraq war, for example, the U.S. sent a CODEL to the Gulf following improvised explosive devices targeted U.S. personnel in armored vehicles, Farkas recalled. The vehicles were not capable of deflecting the explosives, and following a tour of U.S. military sites, Congress conducted a bipartisan effort to ramp up production of the vehicles.

“It’s legitimate, and also necessary and desirable, for members of Congress to go even during a hot war,” Farkas said.

The Pentagon also has some legitimate reasons for turning lawmakers away from military bases, Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and former director for the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, told Fortune.

Hosting a CODEL requires resources like military aircraft and personnel to protect and move lawmakers. In a military theater, armed forces may be unable to spare resources, and when specific threats are made against the military, both troops and elected representatives can be put in harm’s way. In 2016 under then-President Barack Obama, the military asked Congress to limit visits to Afghanistan during a fighting season, though it was not an express ban. Across both Republican and Democrat administrations, U.S. Central Command has ordered limited visits to military sites.

However, Hegseth’s prohibition of military visits has continued, even after the end of “Operation Epic Fury” in May, and when, prior to this month, the last known U.S. attack on Iran was in September. Typically, restrictions are lifted after “hot phases” of conflict end, and the Pentagon’s decision to turn away legislators even during lulls in attacks is what raised suspicions of ulterior motives beyond protecting troops and lawmakers.

Sources indicate that “The big concern I would have is, the administration has noted that Operation Epic Fury is over. Is this more of a lack of transparency and an attempt to hide some of the things that are going on, like the destruction of some of the bases?” Dent said.

Industry observers note that what has lawmakers and former Pentagon officials scratching their heads is that increased transparency to Congress usually yields additional funding, which appears aligned with Hegseth’s push for a record-setting Pentagon budget in fiscal 2027. The government faces a Dec. 11 funding deadline to pass either full-year appropriations or a stopgap measure through the end of the year.

Industry observers note that “Shutting Congress out is not the way to achieve your objectives if you are the Department of Defense,” Farkas said. “If anything, it’s almost a guarantee that you won’t achieve your objectives because Congress understands what their rights and prerogatives are…so that can just erode trust and confidence further.”.

In a recent development, particularly after the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, incoming legislators are going to approach the Pentagon’s steep demands with even more rigor, Fargas noted. President Donald Trump will be reluctant to exercise a veto on the National Defense Authorization Act because it outlines military funding, despite Democrats being likely to make changes to it.

“It’s better to be open and honest,” she stated. “You can’t hide these things anyway. You’re going to bring in contractors. You’re going to have to put out bids for repairs. Somewhere this information is going to come to light.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

According to recent reports, on Zcash Community Forum, a new grant application has emerged which is aimed at making Zcash even more private on iPhone-based wallets. The author seeks a $25,000 grant in order to implement a private way of retrieving encrypted transaction memos.

Essentially, the proposal allows hiding which transactions consumers have been looking up, which is a potential deanonymization vector. Considering how Zcash placese itself on the market, revealing any kind of external information is a step which might shorten the distance between a random transaction and a specific user.

The proposal itself won't touch the network or the blockchain behind it as is. It's an improvement of an SDK (Software Development Kit) that will allow developers to use tools that can help make Zcash more privacy-resilient.

Zcash transactions today contain encrypted data called memos. Various wallets read those memos in order to receive information about the transaction. The message itself stays encrypted, so is retrieved data, however, the query itself is not protected by any means which enables potential tracing.

Even when using Tor, the transaction ID stay out in the open and can be read by anyone.

With the integration of private information retrieval into SDK, hiding the query itself wil be easier, messages would be decrypted locally and wallets themselves will verify the returned information.

The first tests have already shown promising results. During testing in an iOS Simulator, the modified SDK managed to retrieve a 512-byte memo through an encrypted query, without revealing the transaction ID to the wallet server.

The developer expects the implementation of the proposal by January 30, 2027, with testing on physical iPhones and a public SDK release planned for the final stage.

However, the proposal is still seeking funding, and its actual adoption will depend on individual wallet developers.

Industry leaders point to better data, faster learning cycles and closer connections between computation and experimentation as critical to translating AI-designed molecules into development decisions.

In a recent development, LONDON, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI drug discovery is shifting from a race to design faster to a race to learn faster. As AI expands the speed and scale of design, the advantage increasingly lies with those who can turn those designs into validated biological evidence that informs decisions and improves models.

That was the central proposition GenScript Biotech Corporation put to leaders from pharma, AI-native biotechnology, investment and science funding at the 2026 GenScript Biotech Global Forum London. Held during the week of the Jefferies London Healthcare Conference under the theme "AI, Biotech & Capital," the forum brought together executives from Eli Lilly and Firm, Latent Labs, Sofinnova Partners, Basecamp Research, ARIA and GenScript to explore where AI is already creating scientific and economic value, where biology remains a limiting factor, and what evidence will be required as AI-generated possibilities move closer to development.

From AI Possibility to Biological Evidence.

Sources indicate that panelists included Alan Belicha, PhD, Senior Director, Ecosystem Growth and Contributor Partnerships at Eli Lilly and Tech giant; Simon Kohl, PhD, Founder and CEO of Latent Labs; Edward Kliphuis, Partner at Sofinnova Partners; Richard Pearce, Chief Business Officer at Basecamp Research; and Maximilian Sichrovsky, PhD, Science & Technology Lead at ARIA. GenScript was represented by Ray Chen, PhD, President of GenScript Life Science Group; Zhenyan Yan, PhD, Vice President of Corporate Development & Strategy; and Aylin Kosova Bilgin, Chief Marketing and Corporate Communications Officer.

Their discussion highlighted three forces shaping the next phase of AI-enabled drug discovery:.

According to recent reports, AI is moving into harder biology. Kohl described how quickly AI-enabled protein design is evolving, with the field moving beyond binding toward more complex modalities and questions of developability. Even with that progress, he said, the critical gap lies between generating a promising binder and developing a candidate a organization is prepared to advance toward the clinic. Closing it requires addressing biological properties that are harder to model and more difficult to characterize experimentally. "This is all about building AI platforms that advance our partners' portfolios, our partners' programs," added Kohl. "Increasingly, we're betting on both building generative models and the agents around them to create end-to-end workflows. I think that's the exciting moment in time. It feels a lot like what GPT-3 felt like in language. That's what this field is now undergoing, and we couldn't be more excited for what's to come over the next one to two years.".

Data quality and biological relevance are becoming more vital. Panelists pointed to two related gaps: the need for datasets that support biologically relevant predictions, rather than simply more data, and the need for people who can bridge AI and wet-lab biology. As models take on harder biological questions, closer connections between dataset design, experimentation and computation will be critical to generating evidence that improves predictions and informs development decisions.

Industry observers note that capital follows evidence, not design volume. Pearce noted that AI is becoming effective at specific discovery tasks and could allow companies to reach the clinic with less capital than a traditional biotech would need. Long-term value, however, will depend on whether promising molecules can progress beyond design and through development, where biological and ultimately clinical evidence determines which ones move forward. As candidate generation accelerates, the evidence behind each candidate becomes more consequential in determining where development resources and capital are committed. "Ultimately, we're all paying for healthcare, and healthcare costs keep going up. And most development costs are actually going toward drugs that fail; the industry needs to think differently so that environment can change," Pearce added. "I think we're at the point where, with a better understanding of patient biology and stratification, fresh business models will evolve. Compared to other industries that have changed business models, the pharma industry is still doing the same thing it did 70 years ago: discovering a compound, doing a clinical trial, and hoping it works. In 20 years' time, I think that will have changed â and we will know that a new therapy works for a specific individual.".

Turning Faster Design into Faster Learning.

For GenScript, these themes converge around learning velocity: connecting AI-driven design with synthesis, expression, biological testing and usable data to shorten the path from computational possibility to experimental evidence. As discovery cycles accelerate, researchers also need the scientific depth and biological context to interpret that evidence and make informed development decisions.

Recent findings suggest that the shift is already reflected in GenScript's AI drug discovery (AIDD) business, which doubled year over year to $37.8 million in revenue in the first half of 2026. As AI-native companies and pharmaceutical teams move toward larger experimental cycles and more extensive biological characterization, the need for high-quality experimental evidence is growing.

Recent findings suggest that "The data we generate has two crucial purposes: to help advance promising candidates and to feed what we learn back into the next cycle," noted Chen. "As AI allows us to explore more targets, modalities and deeper biology, generating decision-ready data becomes even more important. AI advances discovery. Biology advances AI. GenScript powers the cycle.".

The GenScript Biotech Global Forum is GenScript's thought-leadership platform for bringing together leaders across science, technology, biotechnology and investment to examine the trends reshaping life sciences innovation.

Recent findings suggest that "This conversation doesn't stop in London," added Chen. "We'll continue it in San Francisco during JPM Week because the questions ahead are bigger than any one company or discipline. Progress will depend on how effectively AI, biology and capital come together to accelerate learning and translate scientific possibility into better medicines.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal jury in Latest York convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts Tuesday, including bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Yet Huawei was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.

Sources indicate that the verdict caps a U.S. case introduced in 2018 that accused the Chinese telecommunications giant of misleading banks about its business in Iran while stealing trade secrets from U.S. companies. Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027.

In a recent development, “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a statement.

Industry observers note that “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies,” he added.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that the acquittal on the racketeering charge reflected the manufacturer’s “good-faith compliance culture.”.

“We fully expect to appeal,” Heberlig told reporters, according to Reuters.

In a statement, Huawei argued that the acquittal on the racketeering charge “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis.” The company also remarked it believed the other charges “are equally without legal or factual merit,” and that it would “take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and the daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, was arrested in Canada in December 2018 at the request of U.S. authorities. Prosecutors accused her of misleading banks about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, a subsidiary operating in Iran. After nearly three years fighting extradition, she was released in September 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. prosecutors; the charges were later dismissed.

Separately, the U.S. Commerce Department placed Huawei on its Entity List in 2019, restricting its access to American goods, software, and technology. Washington tightened those controls in 2020 to cover certain foreign-made products manufactured using U.S. technology or software.

According to recent reports, tuesday’s verdict is unlikely to slow Huawei, says Dexter Tiff Roberts, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub. “Huawei has already weathered years of sanctions and still been able to grow and develop remarkably, even with limited access to a number of developed country markets and in particular the U.S.”.

Beijing may double down on Huawei instead, he adds. “In some ways, the adversity it’s already faced with sanctions [has] made Beijing double down on supporting it as a national champion, and if anything, the latest court ruling will only strengthen Beijing’s resolve to support Huawei to ensure it does not stumble.”.

The verdict comes as Huawei takes on a growing role in China’s push to build a domestic AI-computing industry, amid U.S. export controls blocking the country’s access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. The organization’s Ascend semiconductors are China’s best hope for the AI processors needed to train and run models. Chinese models are increasingly being designed to run on Huawei chips, even if Nvidia’s are better for training.

Huawei rotating chair Eric Xu stated the firm cannot produce enough AI chips and servers to meet demand in mainland China. “Since we don’t have enough capacity to even satisfy the demand in China, we don’t have a plan to expand into the international market in a fully fledged way,” Xu told reporters at Huawei Connect in Shanghai in September, according to Reuters.

Huawei reported 880.9 billion yuan ($126 billion) in revenue last year, according to its annual report.

#110556. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (849 w)

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • According to recent reports, in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

According to recent reports, in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley noted that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals concern ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Sources indicate that could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

In a recent development, each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal upgrade at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Sources indicate that last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella notes his organization’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

Recent findings suggest that A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he mentioned at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

According to recent reports, it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t upgrade for the next five to 10 years.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

In a recent development, there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1359 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • Sources indicate that most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves.
  • According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to upcoming institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Sources indicate that most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to upcoming institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The firm claims R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

According to recent reports, the project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery remarked the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the firm, cost nothing.

Recent findings suggest that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as latest rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

It has been revealed that the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

Sources indicate that the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In a recent development, in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

Industry observers note that eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

According to recent reports, eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

Industry observers note that for everyday people, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

Industry observers note that the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

David Schwartz, CTO Emeritus at Ripple and one of the creators of the XRP Ledger, has once again commented on his XRP and Bitcoin sales. This time, the reason was a viral post on X that claimed he had sold almost all of his crypto over the last few months.

According to the post, Schwartz's portfolio reportedly went from 26 million XRP, 1,500 BTC and 40,000 ETH to just 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH. The author called it "an insane reduction" and also referred to Schwartz as the current CTO of Ripple, while he now holds the emeritus title.

Recent findings suggest that schwartz replied that the timeline in the post was wrong. "That wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade," he wrote. As proof, he shared his own post from April 21, 2019. In that post, Schwartz said he was still sticking to the "de-risking strategy" that he and his wife agreed on when they first decided to put their own money into crypto. He also admitted back then that selling during the bull run "still hurt.".

At the same time, Schwartz did not dispute the numbers themselves. "But it's basically true. I hate risk. I can't help it," he wrote in a follow-up post. According to him, pretty much every big risk he has ever taken has worked out well, and rationally he should be taking more risk as he gets wealthier. "But I hate it. I just hate risk and can't do anything about it," Schwartz added.

That wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade. You can find me talking about this in many posts over the years, like this one:https://t.co/5MgcPZ5qyG.

Industry observers note that at press time, XRP was trading at around $0.939, Bitcoin at $61,477 and Ethereum at $1,722. At these prices, the remaining 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH are worth about $2.89 million, and XRP accounts for more than 97% of this sum.

For comparison, at current prices, the peak holdings mentioned in the post would be worth over $185 million, with Bitcoin alone accounting for about half of it.

According to recent reports, schwartz has already explained his sales several times this year. In May, he said he did not have much XRP left and had tried to move most of his assets, other than Ripple stock, away from crypto exposure. In July, he said he regrets selling XRP at $0.10 and ETH at around $1, but noted that he and his wife had agreed to sell at every upcoming all-time high.

According to recent reports, earlier in November, Schwartz disclosed that he sold about 2.5 million XRP in 2025. Per Schwartz, most of these tokens were received in 2020 and 2023, and he paid approximately $1.7 million in capital gains tax on those sales. He shared this in response to a user who called XRP a "terrible investment.".

Among other things, Schwartz has previously said that his main exposure to the crypto sector now comes through Ripple stock, not XRP. In March, Ripple launched a share buyback of up to $750 million that valued the company at $50 billion.

ATLANTA, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Femto Sensing International (www.femtosensing.com), a wholly owned subsidiary of Technica Optical Components (www.technicasa.com) has completed its Atlanta, USA, based manufacturing facility expansion to adapt to increasing demand for its solid-state Optical Sensing FBG Interrogators. The recent doubling of its Atlanta facility's production capacity places the firm in a strong position to meet planned FBG Interrogators manufacturing for 2027 and beyond.

Whether ultra-high performance or a most competitive commercial entry FBG Interrogator is the goal, customers will find an exciting optical sensing solution at Femto Sensing International.

Femto Sensing International offers commercial grade highly accurate FBG Interrogators with scanning ranges from 30nm to 160nm. The firm's portfolio includes the FAZT E Series, M Series, S Series, and the rapidly growing W Series Models of Interrogators: https://femtosensing.com/fbg-monitoring-instruments/.

To fully benefit from Femto Sensing International's FBG Interrogator hardware platforms, the tech giant also provides a world-class matching software platform, comprising of PicoSense X, PCS Logger, MODBUS TCP support, and a built-in Web Backend Server for the M Series and W Series Interrogators, FemtoSense for its FAZT E Series Interrogators, and NanoSense for its S Series Interrogators, all free of charge: https://femtosensing.com/ecosystem-for-m-series-fbg-interrogators/.

Industry observers note that femto Sensing International FBG Interrogators are designed and manufactured in USA and in Canada, and are used in many industries to support both the development and commercial installation of Fiber Bragg Grating Sensors based Optical Sensing Solutions worldwide. The markets addressed include energy and power monitoring, structural health monitoring, aerospace, transportation, marine, industrial, medical, security, civil, and high-performance vehicles, vessels, and structures. Femto Sensing International's growing applications include sensing in high-temperature environments to 1000 Celsius, in cryogenic environments to -270 Celsius, in radiation environments, in chemical environments, and in remote otherwise un-accessible environments.

Recent findings suggest that femto Sensing International is a world leader in the fiber optic sensing industry, with a focus on Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG) Interrogators. The company supports its customers by continuously developing its team and diligently enhancing its manufacturing technologies through innovations and partnerships worldwide.

According to recent reports, FSI's mission is to provide the highest quality and performance FBG Interrogators to meet or exceed customer requirements across a variety of industries. An ISO9001 certified firm, FSI achieves this by making quality its number one priority, delivering products and services on time, reducing costs, and releasing products that are superior to the competition.

Recent findings suggest that FSI is committed to providing state-of-the-art FBG monitoring instruments, and its vision is to make premium performance optical sensing affordable for a growing number of applications. Its solid-state designs are scalable for mass production, with volume-driven cost reductions passed directly to its customers.
