In a recent development, crypto entered the week already wounded. Bitcoin had plunged to a multi-year low near $55,000 over the prior weekend, wiping out leveraged positions and leaving the market in extreme fear territory.

Monday brought a sharp relief rally. Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sent the chipmaker’s shares soaring more than 30% and lifted the Nasdaq by around 7%. Risk assets broadly benefited, and Bitcoin briefly joined the party, climbing toward $64,000.

That bounce proved short-lived. By Tuesday morning, the gains had been fully erased. Bitcoin lagged the equity rebound significantly; Nvidia recovered most of its recent losses, while crypto reclaimed only a fraction of its slide. The divergence highlighted that crypto’s problems run deeper than a single day’s equity news.

Several concrete developments converged to pressure prices. First, the Nvidia-driven rally simply faded. Stock futures turned lower on Tuesday as the initial euphoria cooled.

Recent findings suggest that nasdaq-100 futures dropped around 1%, and related AI and crypto-adjacent equities gave back part of Monday’s gains. Crypto, which had been riding the coattails of the tech surge, sold off in sympathy but more sharply.

Second, institutional flows remained deeply negative. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $570M in net outflows on Monday, the fifth consecutive session of withdrawals.

BlackRock’s IBIT alone accounted for more than $500M of that figure. November’s cumulative outflows reached roughly $4.71Bn, setting a monthly record and removing a major source of structural demand that had previously supported prices.

Third, derivatives markets amplified the move. More than $800M in crypto futures positions were liquidated over the 24-hour period, more than triple the prior day’s total. Forced selling from both long and short positions created a self-reinforcing cascade as prices fell.

Broader macro factors also weighed on sentiment. Markets continue to price in a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with key inflation data (PCE) due shortly.

Higher rates typically pressure non-yielding assets such as Bitcoin. Additional reports of possible upcoming U.S. tariff measures added another layer of risk-off caution. Lingering effects from the large Binance-related hack earlier in the period further eroded confidence in the sector.

Crypto’s decline today is not the result of a single dramatic headline. Instead, it reflects a short-term relief rally that failed to overcome persistent structural headwinds.

It has been revealed that the Nvidia news provided temporary momentum, but without positive ETF flows or a meaningful shift in monetary expectations, that momentum evaporated promptly. Leveraged traders were caught offside, and the resulting liquidations accelerated the drop.

It has been revealed that sentiment remains extremely cautious. The Fear & Greed Index sits deep in extreme fear, at around 10/100, and Bitcoin has still only recovered a modest portion of its November losses.

While some long-term holders and selective buyers may view current levels as attractive, the immediate market is dominated by risk reduction and profit-taking after the failed bounce.

Crypto is down today primarily because Monday’s Nvidia-fueled rally proved unsustainable. Heavy, record-setting Bitcoin ETF outflows continued to drain demand, while a surge in futures liquidations forced additional selling.

Recent findings suggest that macro uncertainty around interest rates and risk assets provided no supporting backdrop. In short, the market tested a bounce, found insufficient real buying interest, and retreated—leaving Bitcoin back below $60,000 and the broader crypto complex lower.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America is approaching a “dangerous moment” for defense spending, according to a new report from Brookings. The think tank warns that rising outlays on Medicaid, Medicare, Social Security, and interest on the $40 trillion national debt are squeezing the military’s share of federal spending.The analysis, published at the start of this week, finds that since 1962 defense spending has been squeezed from 49% to 13% of the federal budget.Defense spending accounted for 2.8% of U.S. GDP in 2026 and is expected to remain at approximately 3% through 2030. This would put defense spending at its lowest share of GDP since World War II, stated Brookings—a nonprofit public policy think tank based in D.C.

Projections that spending will remain relatively constrained are particularly concerning, Brookings’ Jessica Riedl writes. The U.S. is engaged in a conflict in the Middle East with Iran and its proxy groups, and Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a land war that has continued since Russia’s 2022 invasion.

In a recent development, three years ago, the RAND National Security Research Division—a Pentagon research advisor—warned that “in many ways, China is outpacing the United States and has largely negated the U.S. military advantage in the Western Pacific through two decades of focused military investment.”.

Without “significant change” in policy, the “balance of power will continue to shift in China’s favor,” the congressional report found.

And yet, in the years since, the factors stacking up against increased defense spending are only getting weightier.

The Congressional Budget Office’s latest roundup of government spending reveals that $917 billion was spent on defense for fiscal year 2026, a 5.8% increase of $48 billion from the prior year.

It has been revealed that the total for the government’s largest mandatory spending programs (Social Security benefits, Medicare, and Medicaid) came in at nearly $3.5 trillion, a $217 billion uptick on the year before and a 6.7% increase. The government ran a total deficit of $1.9 trillion, the CBO reported, adding to the current national debt burden of $40.7 trillion, per the latest Treasury data.

That debt comes at a cost. Interest payments rise as the government borrows more, particularly when borrowing costs remain elevated. The CBO remarked that for fiscal year 2026, the Treasury paid $1.14 trillion in net interest on the public debt—an 11.1% or $114 billion increase on the previous fiscal year.

According to recent reports, interest payments on the debt are a growing concern for D.C. policymakers. The U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee (JEC) published a report in October that found interest payments in the future could consume more than half of available federal tax receipts by 2036.

Industry observers note that JEC chairman David Schweikert noted: “Under this higher interest rate scenario, we could spend $23 trillion on interest alone over the next decade. That is spending not on Social Security, not on Medicare, not on national defense, but simply paying for yesterday’s borrowing.”.

Sources indicate that the next Congress faces difficult choices: The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget has a countdown to when the combined trust funds of the Social Security system will be forced to start cutting benefits. The countdown right now stands at seven years and six months.

“The newly elected Congress—which controls the purse strings—faces difficult fiscal choices that will persist into the next presidential administration,” the Brookings report states. “Now, there is little headroom in the budget to increase defense spending to meet the proliferating defense challenges … Something will have to give. The advocates of a robust military and American global leadership should prepare to make the most of limited budgetary resources.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • Industry observers note that the most key words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

Industry observers note that the most key words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division remarked it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

Sources indicate that it also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Recent findings suggest that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

Sources indicate that the staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

Sources indicate that that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to owners.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Recent findings suggest that legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself claims the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the challenges presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

According to recent reports, in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

Recent findings suggest that for a organization, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

Industry observers note that that sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

It has been revealed that the harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

GTA VI was built by hand. The man who ran Take-Two during GTA IV says AI could let a filmmaker make the next breakout game

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI, on track to be the biggest entertainment launch of any kind, was made the old-fashioned way: Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick noted in February that Rockstar Games built the game without generative AI.
  • “With regards to GTA 6, generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building.
  • It has been revealed that that’s not to say it didn’t take time and money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI, on track to be the biggest entertainment launch of any kind, was made the old-fashioned way: Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick noted in February that Rockstar Games built the game without generative AI.

“With regards to GTA 6, generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building. Their worlds are handcrafted. That’s what differentiates them,” Zelnick told GamesIndustry.biz. “They’re built from the ground up, building by building, street by street, neighborhood by neighborhood.”.

It has been revealed that that’s not to say it didn’t take time and money. Analysts estimate Take-Two spent more than a billion dollars on the game, which came out more than 13 years after its predecessor (Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick never confirmed the amount but admitted the game was “expensive”). But the next blockbuster video game might come sooner, cheaper—and with an even more cinematic lens, according to Ben Feder, who ran Take-Two Interactive when Grand Theft Auto IV came out in 2008.

“Some great creative mind who would have otherwise gone to make a film will make a video game because it’s as simple as point and click,” Feder noted to Fortune in a long-winding conversation that promptly became more philosophical than experiential about the state of the entertainment industry.

Feder, now managing partner of TIRTA Ventures, noted in a Fortune commentary this month that AI will change how substantial games get made. His firm invests in AI-native game projects. “We put our money where our mouth is,” he said of TIRTA’s investments.

Recent findings suggest that the next great video game maker might be someone who would otherwise have gone into movies, and that’s because AI would make it easier for a filmmaker without a technical background to get into video games. And Feder doesn’t expect that shift to hurt the franchise he once oversaw.

“I don’t think GTA is going anywhere. In fact, it probably goes from strength to strength,” Feder said. “But that’s not to say it’s going to get created in the exact same way that it got created here.”.

In a recent development, video games have long sat at the intersection of the software and entertainment businesses. Feder noted AI will shrink the software side as writing code gets cheaper and easier.

“The argument would be that because AI is making software development commoditized, and software points to zero, it becomes much more about entertainment than it does about both entertainment and computer science,” he said.

Feder described the result as “somewhere between democratizing creativity, the cynic would say commoditizing creativity, but I don’t believe that creativity, true creativity, really gets commoditized unless you’re such a believer in AI that you think AI can also be creative.”.

In a recent development, more games won’t mean more hits. Feder expects a flood of upcoming titles, with only a small share breaking through, and pointed to YouTube.

According to recent reports, “I don’t know how many billions of minutes of video have been on YouTube, but how many of them actually are good? How many of them actually get traction?” he mentioned. “But the ones that do get traction and are good reach billions of people, literally, and can create enormous outcomes, both creatively and commercially.”.

Grand Theft Auto VI shows how large those outcomes can be. Take-Two has not disclosed the game’s cost, though estimates put its development budget at $1 billion to $1.5 billion. Brokerage Oppenheimer projected about $1.85 billion in gross revenue in the game’s first three days, Reuters reported.

“Thirteen years of investment you make back in a day. Unbelievable,” Feder stated. “But it only happens if you create the most awesome game ever.”.

Recent findings suggest that AI tools could change that math across the industry, he remarked. “It’s going to get harder to justify a $2 billion game in a world where the next best alternative is two orders of magnitude less.”.

It has been revealed that GTA VI, ironically, did make back all the money it poured into it, and then some. Feder mentioned that counterargument is a pretty good devil’s advocate. “What’s the argument for not spending another $2 billion on the next one and making it back in a day?” he said. “That’s a valid argument.”.

At this point, the conversation became a lived experience of the entertainment industry at large. While most people think of film and cinema as making up the lion’s share of what people consider entertainment, video games have always been there, and they’ve been blockbusters of their own. But recently, as with movies, it seems big publishers have long concentrated their money on a handful of games, or, as the Marvel Cinematic Universe has shown, on the franchise model.

“Even when I was at Take-Two for GTA IV, we were the first, and others followed, to develop a strategy of fewer, bigger titles,” Feder remarked. And just like movies, the non-Indie games have a tough time breaking through the noise. Feder said the pressure falls on games in the middle, those with major budgets and smaller audiences.

“It’s hard to make the numbers work.”.

Sources indicate that feder said that when he ran Take-Two, he saw the industry’s next frontier as characters that look like movie actors rather than figures in a game. Of GTA VI, he said, “This gets as close to it as I’ve ever seen.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LeBron James skips data roaming and paid apps, yet his $1.4 billion fortune rests on investing in his body and his businesses.
  • Most everyday money advice tells people to cut the small charges they pay again and again, such as roaming fees, app subscriptions and premium tiers of services they already use.
  • James has never kept his thrift a secret.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LeBron James skips data roaming and paid apps, yet his $1.4 billion fortune rests on investing in his body and his businesses.

Most everyday money advice tells people to cut the small charges they pay again and again, such as roaming fees, app subscriptions and premium tiers of services they already use. A person who pays many of them each month can spend a large sum over a year without noticing. That advice is written for households with thin margins, where a few dollars can decide whether a bill gets paid, so it is fair to ask whether it means anything for someone who will never have to worry about money. LeBron James, one of the richest athletes alive, is the sharpest test of that question, because he keeps refusing exactly these charges. He could pay all of them without noticing and still declines. That raises a real question about his fortune: Did the habit help make him rich, or is it simply something he does while being rich?

James has never kept his thrift a secret. He appeared in the 2015 film "Trainwreck," which played his cheapness for laughs, according to CNBC. He chose to make the trait part of his public image, and that makes it read more as a statement of who he is than as a private budgeting system. That matters for how to judge it. A trait someone displays in public can be entirely sincere and still explain very little about where the money came from.

Recent findings suggest that yahoo Sports set out to show how James's frugal habits fit his status as a billionaire, from listening to Pandora with the commercials to skipping data roaming on trips to Toronto. Those habits are real, and he has kept them for years, so they deserve to be taken seriously as a principle he lives by. The harder question is whether a principle about a few dollars has anything to do with a fortune counted in billions. Answering it means weighing the people who credit his thrift for his wealth against the evidence of where James actually spent his money.

James's teammates noticed his thrift in a daily refusal to pay for something most travelers buy without a second thought. On trips into Canada, he kept his phone off cellular data until he reached Wi-Fi at the team hotel or the arena. He chose to stay offline in a foreign city rather than pay extra to use his phone there. His teammates saw the routine most often in Toronto. Kevin Love, James's former Cavaliers teammate, states he watched it happen there more times than he could count. That repetition turns a skipped charge into a rule. A traveler who forgets to switch on roaming once is careless, but a man who waits for Wi-Fi on every trip has made a decision.

The money at stake was trivial, a roaming fee that former NBA player Tristan Thompson estimated at $40, according to Yahoo Sports. To his teammates, the small size of the charge was the whole point. Love links the habit to an old piece of financial wisdom: losses left unchecked can ruin even the largest fortune, however small each one is. In that view, cutting off minor costs is simply what a careful rich person does. Thompson went further and tied the habit directly to James's wealth. "I guess that's what makes him a billionaire," Thompson stated.

That is a claim about cause. It comes from people who watched James on the road but never saw his accounts.

The Toronto routine highlights how James treats a small charge. Whether that habit explains his fortune is still an open question.

LeBron James has claimed his thrift as his own policy, and that puts it on firmer ground than stories told by his teammates. He confirmed the habit himself in a 2017 ESPN interview, Yahoo Sports reports, and he named a short list of small charges he refuses to pay. "No, I'm not doing that. I'm not turning on data roaming, I'm not buying no apps, I still got Pandora with commercials," James stated. He could pay for any premium tier and chose the version with ads instead. The refusal is a choice, not a limit on what he can afford.

Industry observers note that the rule outlasted the interview by years and carried over to a different platform. In March 2023, James publicly refused to pay for Twitter $TWTR Blue, according to CNBC, and he remarked he expected to lose his blue check mark because he would not pay. Tristan Thompson, a former teammate from James's years in Cleveland, states James also sticks with the free version of Spotify $SPOT. James keeps the rule from music to social media, even when it costs him a public mark of status. That makes it a principle he holds, not a running joke.

In a recent development, the sums James turns down are too small to matter to someone with his income. His 2023 tweet put the Twitter Blue fee at $5, though the service cost $8 a month at the time, according to CNBC. Next to his Lakers pay of $52,627,153 for the 2025-26 season, either amount is far too small to change his finances in any way. The refusal saves him no money that counts. Its value is symbolic: it shows he will not pay a few dollars he considers wasted.

If the habit cannot explain the fortune, the answer lies in where James has been willing to spend heavily.

According to recent reports, james refuses small charges, but he spends freely wherever the money can come back to him. His teammates credit the refused fees for his wealth, yet his fortune, an estimated $1.4 billion according to Forbes figures reported by Yahoo Sports, rests on heavy investment in his body and his businesses. One early deal shows how that kind of investment can pay off. James reportedly took home around $30 million from his share of Beats by Dre when Apple $AAPL bought the company in 2014, according to TIME. That is a different discipline from thrift. It is a rule about where his money goes rather than a rule against spending it.

According to recent reports, his spending on his own body, reportedly more than $1 million on health and fitness, looks like a star's indulgence, but it serves the body that earns his salary. James has stretched his career into a 23rd NBA season in 2025-26, according to TIME, and he collects another salary for every year he stays on the court. When James pays for his own upkeep, he is protecting the income his playing career still brings in.

Sources indicate that james has made the same choice again and again, taking a share of a business over a one-time payment. With Beats, he took a small equity stake instead of a fee, according to TIME. In 2021 he gave up his small piece of Liverpool in return for a wider stake in Fenway Sports Group, the tech giant that owns the club along with the Red Sox and the Penguins. His holdings also include SpringHill. Set against that pattern, the refused data fees and app upgrades are a real and lasting principle, but they are not where the billions came from.

He guards a few dollars out of conviction, but he got rich by taking a piece of the business.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • Sources indicate that the outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

Sources indicate that the outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

According to recent reports, the upcoming funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the manufacturer, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the organization-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

Sources indicate that “The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Recent findings suggest that marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Industry observers note that lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders mentioned the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Recent findings suggest that its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders mentioned. A second, larger site using AMD’s latest Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The firm indicates it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a latest AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he remarked.

According to recent reports, that’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe claims gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Industry observers note that competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

According to recent reports, marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

It has been revealed that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe looks to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis remarked. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

Sources indicate that the $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis mentioned. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking tech giant DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Sources indicate that past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis stated the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

In a recent development, ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of upcoming chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

  • While Ethereum remains one of the most affected cryptocurrencies during the prolonged crypto market volatility, the latest data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows a massive slowdown in its exchange outflows.
  • Amid growing market fear, Ethereum outflows from Binance over the last month have hit a historic low as investors continue to move fewer ETH tokens away from the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As demand for major crypto assets has increased, Ethereum remains on hold amid growing market fear and uncertainty, while exchange activities across the broad crypto market are showing a bearish trend.

While Ethereum remains one of the most affected cryptocurrencies during the prolonged crypto market volatility, the latest data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows a massive slowdown in its exchange outflows.

Amid growing market fear, Ethereum outflows from Binance over the last month have hit a historic low as investors continue to move fewer ETH tokens away from the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.

The data shows that about 3.58 million ETH have been withdrawn from Binance over the last 30 days, marking an all-time low in Ethereum outflows on the exchange.

Further data demonstrates that the decline has come as Ethereum continues to struggle to stabilize its price and continues to weaken, trading around the $1,700 mark.

It is vital to note that the decline in exchange outflows is expected, considering the growing market weakness and negative shift in investor sentiment over the period.

However, the metric has drawn different attention from market participants, given expectations that the massive security breach Binance suffered should trigger large withdrawals from the exchange.

Although blockchain trackers recently identified multiple large Ethereum withdrawals by the Binance hacker, it appears that the moves did not materialize into increased Ethereum outflows.

Apart from the attackers' withdrawals, it appears that Ethereum holders on the exchange did not respond to the attack in the conventional way, as security incidents like this often make investors more cautious and wary about keeping their assets on the exchange.

While this typically prompts them to transfer the assets into private wallets where they have greater control, it appears that Ethereum holders remained comfortable with keeping their funds on the exchange.

Tech Report: Island is a latest screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A fresh startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time.
  • This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.
  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A fresh startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a major mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

Recent findings suggest that “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

Sources indicate that “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping owners meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team claims that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Sources indicate that island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into owners’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage consumers to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Recent findings suggest that similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup indicates Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The manufacturer hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but intends to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.
